title: Lecture 20: Covariance Estimation for Low-Dimensional Data
text: Lecture 9 proved that \(m\gtrsim n\) samples estimate an \(n\)-dimensional covariance matrix in operator norm, and observed that the bound charges for all \(n\) directions even when the data are concentrated near a low-dimensional subspace. The net argument could not do better, because the net of the sphere has \(e^{cn}\) points whatever \(\Sigma\) is. The matrix deviation inequality of Lecture 19 replaces the net by the Gaussian width of the relevant index set, and the relevant set is an ellipsoid whose width is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}\) rather than \(\sqrt{n\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\). The result is the theorem stated without proof in Lecture 9: the sample size that matters is the effective rank \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma/\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), not the dimension.

title: Lecture 20: Covariance Estimation for Low-Dimensional Data
text:
1 The deviation of squares
The covariance error is a quadratic form in the data, so the first step is to pass from \(\|Ax\|_2-\sqrt m\|x\|_2\) to its square. Throughout, \(A\) is an \(m\times n\) matrix with independent, mean-zero, isotropic, \(K\)-subgaussian rows, as in Lectures 9 and 19, and for bounded \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) we write \(w(T)\) for the Gaussian width and \(\operatorname{rad}(T)=\sup_{x\in T}\|x\|_2\).

Proposition 1 (Deviation of squares) For every bounded \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T}\Big|\|Ax\|_2^2-m\|x\|_2^2\Big|
\leq CK^2\big(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T)\big)^2+CK\sqrt m\operatorname{rad}(T)\big(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T)\big).
\]







NoteProof





Write \(X_x=\|Ax\|_2-\sqrt m\|x\|_2\) and \(S=\sup_{x\in T}|X_x|\). Since \(a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)\) and \(\|Ax\|_2+\sqrt m\|x\|_2\leq|X_x|+2\sqrt m\|x\|_2\), \[
\Big|\|Ax\|_2^2-m\|x\|_2^2\Big|=|X_x|\big(\|Ax\|_2+\sqrt m\|x\|_2\big)
\leq S^2+2\sqrt m\operatorname{rad}(T)\,S
\] for every \(x\in T\). By the tail form of the matrix deviation inequality (Lecture 19), \(S\leq CK(1+u)(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T))\) with probability at least \(1-2e^{-u^2}\), so \(S\) has a sub-Gaussian tail at scale \(CK(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T))\), and integrating gives \(\mathbb ES^2\leq CK^2(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T))^2\) and \(\mathbb ES\leq CK(w(T)+\operatorname{rad}(T))\). Take expectations.



The two terms have different origins. The first, of order \(K^2w(T)^2\), is the square of the deviation of the norm process and does not grow with \(m\). The second, of order \(\sqrt m\cdot Kw(T)\), is the cross term between the deviation and the typical size \(\sqrt m\|x\|_2\) of \(\|Ax\|_2\). After division by \(m\), they become the \(r/m\) and \(\sqrt{r/m}\) terms of the covariance bound.

title: Lecture 20: Covariance Estimation for Low-Dimensional Data
text:
2 Covariance estimation with effective rank

Definition 1 (Effective rank) The effective rank of a nonzero positive semidefinite matrix \(\Sigma\) is \[
r(\Sigma):=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}}=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i(\Sigma)}{\max_i\lambda_i(\Sigma)}\in[1,n].
\]

The effective rank is \(n\) when all eigenvalues are equal and stays bounded when the eigenvalues decay quickly. It is the stable rank of \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) in the sense of Lecture 13, since \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma\) and \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), and up to a constant it is the stable dimension of the ellipsoid \(\Sigma^{1/2}B_2^n\), whose width is \(\mathbb E\|\Sigma^{1/2}g\|_2\leq\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}\) and whose radius is \(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}\). Unlike the rank, it is continuous in \(\Sigma\).

Theorem 1 (Covariance estimation for low-dimensional data) Let \(X\) be a mean-zero random vector in \(\mathbb R^n\) with covariance \(\Sigma\), and suppose that for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) the marginal \(\langle X,x\rangle\) is \(K\langle\Sigma x,x\rangle\)-subgaussian. Let \(\Sigma_m\) be the sample covariance of \(m\) independent copies of \(X\). Then \[
\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq CK^2\Big(\sqrt{\frac{r(\Sigma)}m}+\frac{r(\Sigma)}m\Big)\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}} .
\]







NoteProof





As in Lecture 9, write \(X_i=\Sigma^{1/2}Z_i\) with \(Z_i\) independent, isotropic, \(K\)-subgaussian, and let \(A\) be the matrix with rows \(Z_i^{\mathsf T}\); if \(\Sigma\) is singular, work in its range. Then \(\Sigma_m-\Sigma=\Sigma^{1/2}(\frac1mA^{\mathsf T}A-I)\Sigma^{1/2}\), and since this matrix is symmetric its operator norm is the supremum of the absolute value of its quadratic form over the sphere: \[
\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}
=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\Big|\Big\langle\Big(\frac1mA^{\mathsf T}A-I\Big)\Sigma^{1/2}x,\Sigma^{1/2}x\Big\rangle\Big|
=\sup_{y\in\mathcal E}\Big|\frac1m\|Ay\|_2^2-\|y\|_2^2\Big|,
\] where \(\mathcal E:=\Sigma^{1/2}S^{n-1}\) is an ellipsoid. This is the whole point: the net argument of Lecture 9 evaluated the same quadratic form on the sphere, where every direction costs the same, whereas here it is evaluated on \(\mathcal E\), whose extent in each direction is the standard deviation of the data in that direction.
Now apply Proposition 1 to \(T=\mathcal E\). Its width is \[
w(\mathcal E)=\mathbb E\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\langle g,\Sigma^{1/2}x\rangle=\mathbb E\|\Sigma^{1/2}g\|_2
\leq\big(\mathbb E\|\Sigma^{1/2}g\|_2^2\big)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma},
\] and its radius is \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}\). Writing \(\sigma=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) and \(r=r(\Sigma)\), so that \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=r\sigma\) and \(\sqrt{r\sigma}+\sqrt\sigma\leq2\sqrt{r\sigma}\) because \(r\geq1\), \[
\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\frac1m\Big[CK^2\cdot4r\sigma+CK\sqrt m\sqrt\sigma\cdot2\sqrt{r\sigma}\Big]
=C'\sigma\Big[K^2\frac rm+K\sqrt{\frac rm}\Big],
\] and \(K\leq K^2\) since \(K\geq1\).



Compare with Lecture 9, whose bound was the same with \(n\) in place of \(r(\Sigma)\). Since \(r(\Sigma)\leq n\) always, the new theorem is never worse, and it is much better when the spectrum of \(\Sigma\) decays.






NoteWhat the effective rank buys





Relative error. For \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\varepsilon\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) as soon as \(m\geq CK^4r(\Sigma)/\varepsilon^2\). The ambient dimension has disappeared from the sample complexity.
Fast spectral decay. If \(\lambda_i(\Sigma)\leq\lambda_1i^{-2}\), then \(r(\Sigma)\leq\pi^2/6\), and a number of samples independent of \(n\) estimates \(\Sigma\) to any fixed relative accuracy, in dimension \(n=10^6\) as well as in dimension \(10\). The estimate is in operator norm, so it controls the leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) through the Davis–Kahan theorem, which is what principal component analysis needs.
Spiked covariance. If \(\Sigma=I_n+\theta vv^{\mathsf T}\) for a unit vector \(v\) and \(\theta>0\), then \(r(\Sigma)=(n+\theta)/(1+\theta)\), which is about \(n/\theta\) for large \(\theta\). A strong spike reduces the effective rank, and the theorem says the spike direction is learned from \(m\gtrsim n/\theta\) samples, up to the accuracy needed for Davis–Kahan.
Two regimes. For \(m\geq r\) the bound is \(\sqrt{r/m}\), the parametric rate for \(r\) effective parameters. For \(m<r\) it is \(r/m>1\), which is worse than the trivial bound \(\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|\Sigma_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) only by a constant, and reflects that \(\Sigma_m\) has rank at most \(m\).









NoteSharpness, and the tail





For Gaussian data the theorem is sharp in both terms: Koltchinskii and Lounici (Koltchinskii and Lounici 2017) proved matching lower bounds, so that \(\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\asymp(\sqrt{r/m}+r/m)\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) for \(X\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), and they showed that \(\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) concentrates around its mean at the scale \(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}(\sqrt{1/m}+1/m)\), much smaller than the mean itself when \(r\) is large. A high-probability version of the theorem above, with \(r+u^2\) in place of \(r\) on an event of probability \(1-2e^{-u^2}\), follows by running the proof with the tail form of the matrix deviation inequality instead of its expectation.




Koltchinskii, Vladimir, and Karim Lounici. 2017. “Concentration Inequalities and Moment Bounds for Sample Covariance Operators.” Bernoulli 23 (1): 110–33. https://doi.org/10.3150/15-BEJ730.

title: Lecture 20: Covariance Estimation for Low-Dimensional Data
text:
3 Random projections, revisited
The same inequality sharpens the random projection theorem of Lecture 13.

Proposition 2 (Sizes of random projections, sharp constant) Let \(A\) have independent, mean-zero, isotropic, \(K\)-subgaussian rows and let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be bounded. Then \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(AT)\leq\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)+CKw(T).
\]







NoteProof





Apply the matrix deviation inequality (Lecture 19) to the set \(T-T\), for which \(\operatorname{rad}(T-T)=\operatorname{diam}(T)\) and \(w(T-T)=2w(T)\): \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(AT)=\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T-T}\|Ax\|_2
\leq\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)+\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T-T}\Big|\|Ax\|_2-\sqrt m\|x\|_2\Big|
\leq\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)+CK\big(2w(T)+\operatorname{diam}(T)\big),
\] and \(\operatorname{diam}(T)\leq C'w(T)\): for any \(x,y\in T\), by the symmetrization identity of Lecture 3, \(w(T)=\tfrac12w(T-T)\geq\tfrac12\mathbb E|\langle g,x-y\rangle|=\tfrac12\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\|x-y\|_2\), and one takes the supremum over \(x,y\).



Lecture 13 had \(C(w(T)+\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T))\) with an unspecified constant in front of the \(\sqrt m\) term, and only for Gaussian matrices. Here the leading term has constant exactly \(1\), the matrix need only have sub-Gaussian rows, and the price is the width of \(T\) with no factor of \(\sqrt m\). In the regime \(m\gtrsim d(T)\) of Lecture 13, dividing by \(\sqrt m\) shows that \(A/\sqrt m\) changes the diameter of \(T\) by a factor \(1+O(K\sqrt{d(T)/m})\), and the phase transition at the stable dimension is now visible with its constant.

title: Lecture 20: Covariance Estimation for Low-Dimensional Data
text:
4 Where we go next
Two applications of the matrix deviation inequality have now been computed, and both turned a question about a random matrix into a question about the Gaussian width of a set: an ellipsoid for covariance estimation, a difference set for projections. The final application of the course is sparse recovery. There the set is the intersection of the kernel of a random measurement matrix with a set of sparse or nearly sparse vectors, its width is \(\sqrt{s\log(n/s)}\) by Lecture 13, and the inequality yields the number of linear measurements needed to recover an \(s\)-sparse signal by convex optimization.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text: Dudley’s inequality bounds the supremum of a sub-Gaussian process by an entropy integral, and Lecture 16 showed two ways it can fail: Talagrand’s example, where the integral diverges although the supremum is finite, and the \(\ell^1\) ball, where it is off by a logarithm. In both cases the covering numbers are the wrong bookkeeping. They count how many points are needed to approximate \(T\) at scale \(\varepsilon\) uniformly over \(T\), but different parts of \(T\) may need different resolutions at different scales. Generic chaining keeps the chaining argument and changes only the bookkeeping: instead of fixing the scales and asking how many points each needs, it fixes the number of points at each stage and asks, for each \(t\) separately, how well the stages approximate \(t\). The resulting functional \(\gamma_2(T,d)\) is never larger than Dudley’s integral, and for Gaussian processes it is the answer: it is equivalent to \(\mathbb E\sup X\) up to absolute constants.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text:
1 Rewriting Dudley’s sum
Recall the outcome of chaining in Lecture 16. With \(\varepsilon_k=2^{-k}\) and \(T_k\) an \(\varepsilon_k\)-net of minimal size \(N_k=N(T,d,2^{-k})\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq C\sum_k2^{-k}\sqrt{\log N_k}.
\] Each term is the product of a scale and the square root of a log cardinality. Turn the bookkeeping around: fix the cardinalities and let the scales adapt. A sequence of subsets \((T_k)_{k\geq0}\) of \(T\) is admissible if \[
|T_0|=1,
\qquad
|T_k|\leq2^{2^k}\quad(k\geq1).
\] The doubly exponential growth is chosen so that \(\sqrt{\log|T_k|}\leq2^{k/2}\) grows geometrically, which is what makes the sums below converge. Given an admissible sequence, the sets \(T_k\) are nets of \(T\) at the scales \[
\varepsilon_k:=\sup_{t\in T}d(t,T_k),
\qquad d(t,A):=\inf_{a\in A}d(t,a),
\] and running the chaining argument with these nets gives \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq C\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}\sup_{t\in T}d(t,T_k).
\tag{1}\] Taking the infimum over admissible sequences, the right side is equivalent to Dudley’s integral up to constants (see Lemma 1 below for one direction). So far nothing has happened. The change is to move the supremum outside the sum.

Definition 1 (Talagrand’s \(\gamma_2\) functional) For a metric space \((T,d)\), \[
\gamma_2(T,d):=\inf_{(T_k)}\ \sup_{t\in T}\ \sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}d(t,T_k),
\] the infimum over all admissible sequences.

Since \(\sup_t\sum_k\leq\sum_k\sup_t\), the functional is at most the quantity in Equation 1 for every admissible sequence, hence at most Dudley’s sum. The difference is that Dudley charges every \(t\) for the worst-approximated point at each scale, while \(\gamma_2\) charges each \(t\) only for its own approximation errors, and the worst total cost over \(t\) is what counts. In a space where the nets that serve some points well at stage \(k\) already serve other points well at all later stages, this matters.






NoteTalagrand’s example has bounded \(\gamma_2\)





Let \(T=\{0\}\cup\{t_n:n\geq1\}\subseteq\ell^2\) with \(t_n=e_n/\sqrt{1+\log n}\), the set of Lecture 16 with the origin added, which changes neither the supremum of the isonormal process, since \(\sup_nX_{t_n}\geq0\) almost surely, nor the divergence of Dudley’s integral. Take \[
T_k:=\{0\}\cup\{t_n:n\leq2^{2^k}\},
\qquad|T_k|\leq2^{2^k}+1 ,
\] which is admissible after shifting the index by one. For \(t=t_n\), the distance \(d(t_n,T_k)\) is \(0\) once \(2^{2^k}\geq n\), and is at most \(\|t_n\|_2=1/\sqrt{1+\log n}\) always, using the origin. So \[
\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}d(t_n,T_k)\leq\frac1{\sqrt{1+\log n}}\sum_{k:\,2^{2^k}<n}2^{k/2}
\leq\frac{C\,2^{k_n/2}}{\sqrt{1+\log n}},
\] where \(k_n\) is the largest index with \(2^{2^{k_n}}<n\), so that \(2^{k_n}<\log_2n\) and \(2^{k_n/2}<\sqrt{\log_2n}\). The right side is bounded by an absolute constant, uniformly in \(n\), and \(d(0,T_k)=0\). Hence \(\gamma_2(T,d)\leq C\), in agreement with the finiteness of \(\mathbb E\sup_nX_{t_n}\).
The mechanism is visible: the far-out points \(t_n\) with \(n\) huge are approximated by the origin, at a cost \(\|t_n\|_2\) that is tiny, and the stages \(T_k\) with \(2^{2^k}<n\) that fail to contain \(t_n\) are few, about \(\log\log n\) of them, with geometrically growing weights that sum to \(\sqrt{\log n}\). Dudley, by contrast, insisted on covering each \(t_n\) to within \(\varepsilon\) by a point at distance \(\varepsilon\), and paid \(\exp(2/\varepsilon^2)\) points to do so.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text:
2 The generic chaining bound

Theorem 1 (Generic chaining) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) be a centered process, sub-Gaussian with respect to a metric \(d\) for which \((T,d)\) is separable. Then \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq C\gamma_2(T,d),
\] and for every \(t_0\in T\) and \(u\geq0\), with probability at least \(1-2e^{-u^2}\), \[
\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\leq C(1+u)\gamma_2(T,d).
\]







NoteProof





As in Lecture 16 it suffices to treat finite \(T\); the reduction is the same, using that an admissible sequence for \(T\) restricts to one for a subset after replacing each point by a nearest point of the subset, which at most doubles every \(d(t,T_k)\). Fix an admissible sequence \((T_k)\) with \(T_0=\{t_0\}\) and \[
S:=\sup_{t\in T}\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}d(t,T_k)
\] close to \(\gamma_2(T,d)\). For \(t\in T\) let \(\pi_k(t)\in T_k\) be a nearest point, so \(d(t,\pi_k(t))=d(t,T_k)\), and \(\pi_k(t)=t\) for large \(k\) since \(T\) is finite.
Step 1: the chain. \(X_t-X_{t_0}=\sum_{k\geq1}(X_{\pi_k(t)}-X_{\pi_{k-1}(t)})\), a finite sum, with links of \(\psi_2\) norm at most \[
d\big(\pi_k(t),\pi_{k-1}(t)\big)\leq d(t,T_k)+d(t,T_{k-1}).
\]
Step 2: the increments, uniformly. At stage \(k\) the link \((\pi_k(t),\pi_{k-1}(t))\) is one of at most \(|T_k||T_{k-1}|\leq2^{2^{k+1}}\) pairs \((a,b)\). For a single pair and \(s\geq0\), the sub-Gaussian tail of Lecture 5 gives \(\mathbb P\{|X_a-X_b|\geq d(a,b)s\}\leq2e^{-s^2}\). Take \(s_k:=\sqrt{2^{k+2}\log2}+u\), so that \(s_k^2\geq2^{k+2}\log2+u^2\) and the union bound over the pairs at stage \(k\) gives failure probability at most \[
2^{2^{k+1}}\cdot2\exp\big(-2^{k+2}\log2-u^2\big)=2\cdot2^{-2^{k+1}}e^{-u^2}.
\] Summing over \(k\geq1\), all links at all stages satisfy \(|X_a-X_b|\leq d(a,b)s_k\) outside an event of probability at most \(2e^{-u^2}\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-2^{k+1}}\leq2e^{-u^2}\).
Step 3: summing the chain. On the good event, for every \(t\), \[
|X_t-X_{t_0}|\leq\sum_{k\geq1}\big(d(t,T_k)+d(t,T_{k-1})\big)\big(2^{(k+2)/2}\sqrt{\log2}+u\big).
\] The two sums \(\sum_k2^{k/2}d(t,T_k)\) and \(\sum_k2^{k/2}d(t,T_{k-1})=\sqrt2\sum_k2^{(k-1)/2}d(t,T_{k-1})\) are each at most \(\sqrt2\,S\), and since \(2^{k/2}\geq1\) the sums without the weight \(2^{k/2}\) are also at most \(S\). Altogether \(|X_t-X_{t_0}|\leq C(1+u)S\), uniformly in \(t\), which is the tail bound. Integrating in \(u\) and using \(\mathbb EX_{t_0}=0\) gives the expectation bound, and \(S\) may be taken arbitrarily close to \(\gamma_2(T,d)\).



The proof is the proof of Dudley’s inequality with one change: the threshold for the link at stage \(k\) is proportional to the link’s own length \(d(\pi_k(t),\pi_{k-1}(t))\) rather than to the worst link length \(2^{-k+2}\) at that stage. The union bound is unaffected, because the number of pairs at stage \(k\) is controlled by the admissibility condition and not by the scale, and the sum along the chain then produces the \(\gamma_2\) sum for the particular \(t\) rather than Dudley’s sum of suprema.






NoteA sharper tail





The tail bound above has scale \(\gamma_2(T,d)\) in the fluctuation term \(u\gamma_2\), whereas for Gaussian processes Borell–TIS (Lecture 11) gives fluctuations on the smaller scale \(\sigma=\sup_t\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}X_t}\). A more careful choice of chain, in which one moves from \(\pi_{k-1}(t)\) to \(\pi_k(t)\) only when \(d(t,T_k)\) is less than half of \(d(t,\pi_{k-1}(t))\), makes the link lengths decrease geometrically and yields \[
\sup_{s,t\in T}|X_t-X_s|\leq C\big[\gamma_2(T,d)+u\operatorname{diam}(T)\big]
\] with probability at least \(1-2e^{-u^2}\), for every sub-Gaussian process. This is the form in the handwritten notes, and it is the sub-Gaussian analogue of Borell–TIS: the mean is controlled by the geometry through \(\gamma_2\), and the fluctuations by the diameter alone.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text:
3 Comparison with Dudley and Sudakov
Two lemmas place \(\gamma_2\) between the bounds of Lectures 12 and 16.

Lemma 1 (\(\gamma_2\) is at most Dudley’s integral) For every metric space \((T,d)\), \[
\gamma_2(T,d)\leq C\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon .
\]







NoteProof





Assume the integral is finite, so \(T\) is totally bounded. For \(k\geq0\) let \[
\varepsilon_k:=\inf\big\{\varepsilon>0:\ N(T,d,\varepsilon)\leq2^{2^k}\big\},
\] a nonincreasing sequence tending to \(0\), with \(\varepsilon_0\) at most the diameter. Choose \(T_k\) to be a \(2\varepsilon_k\)-net of cardinality at most \(2^{2^k}\), which exists by the definition of \(\varepsilon_k\); then \((T_k)\) is admissible and \(d(t,T_k)\leq2\varepsilon_k\) for every \(t\), so \[
\gamma_2(T,d)\leq2\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}\varepsilon_k .
\] For \(\varepsilon<\varepsilon_k\) we have \(N(T,d,\varepsilon)>2^{2^k}\), so \(\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\geq2^{k/2}\sqrt{\log2}\) on \((\varepsilon_{k+1},\varepsilon_k)\), and \[
\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon
\geq\sqrt{\log2}\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}(\varepsilon_k-\varepsilon_{k+1}).
\] Finally, writing \(\varepsilon_k=\sum_{j\geq k}(\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1})\) and exchanging the order of summation, \[
\sum_{k\geq0}2^{k/2}\varepsilon_k=\sum_{j\geq0}(\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1})\sum_{k\leq j}2^{k/2}
\leq\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2-1}\sum_{j\geq0}2^{j/2}(\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1}),
\] which is at most a constant times the integral.




Lemma 2 (\(\gamma_2\) is at least the Sudakov quantity) For every metric space \((T,d)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[
\gamma_2(T,d)\geq c\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)} .
\]







NoteProof





Let \(N=N(T,d,\varepsilon)\geq2\) and let \((T_k)\) be admissible. Let \(k\) be the largest index with \(2^{2^k}<N\), so that \(2^{2^{k+1}}\geq N\) and hence \(2^{k/2}\geq\sqrt{\log_2N}/2\). Since \(|T_k|<N\), the set \(T_k\) is not an \(\varepsilon\)-net of \(T\), so some \(t\in T\) has \(d(t,T_k)\geq\varepsilon\). For this \(t\), \[
\sum_{j\geq0}2^{j/2}d(t,T_j)\geq2^{k/2}d(t,T_k)\geq\frac{\varepsilon\sqrt{\log_2N}}2 .
\] Taking the supremum over \(t\) and the infimum over admissible sequences gives the claim.



So for a general metric space, \[
c\,\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}
\ \leq\ \gamma_2(T,d)\ \leq\ C\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon ,
\] and both inequalities can be strict. For Talagrand’s example the right side is infinite while \(\gamma_2\) is bounded. For the \(\ell^1\) ball, Lecture 16 found the right side of order \((\log n)^{3/2}\) and the left side of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\); the theorem below shows that \(\gamma_2(B_1^n)\asymp\sqrt{\log n}\), so \(\gamma_2\) sits at the lower bound there and the entropy integral is what overshoots.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text:
4 The majorizing measure theorem
For Gaussian processes the generic chaining bound is sharp.

Theorem 2 (Talagrand’s majorizing measure theorem) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) be a centered Gaussian process with separable canonical metric \(d\). Then \[
c\,\gamma_2(T,d)\leq\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq C\gamma_2(T,d)
\] for absolute constants \(c,C>0\).

The upper bound is Theorem 1, since a Gaussian process is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(2d\). The lower bound is the deep part. It says that for Gaussian processes, chaining is not merely a technique but the only mechanism: whatever makes \(\mathbb E\sup X\) large must be visible as an admissible sequence that cannot approximate some point cheaply. The next lecture proves the lower bound. Its proof reverses the chaining argument, building a tree of subsets of \(T\) whose branches are well separated at each depth and using Sudakov’s minoration, in the sharp form of the Sudakov–Fernique comparison, to show that the process must pay \(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(\text{number of branches})}\) at every branching.
The name comes from Fernique’s original formulation of the lower bound in terms of probability measures on \(T\) (Fernique 1975), and Talagrand’s theorem (Talagrand 1987) established the matching upper bound and the equivalence with the \(\gamma_2\) functional; the modern account is (Talagrand 2014).

Fernique, Xavier. 1975. “Régularité Des Trajectoires Des Fonctions Aléatoires Gaussiennes.” École d’Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour IV, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 480: 1–96.

Talagrand, Michel. 1987. “Regularity of Gaussian Processes.” Acta Mathematica 159: 99–149. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02392556.

Talagrand, Michel. 2014. Upper and Lower Bounds for Stochastic Processes: Modern Methods and Classical Problems. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-54075-2.
Three consequences are worth recording.
Gaussian width is a \(\gamma_2\) functional. For \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with the Euclidean metric, \(w(T)\asymp\gamma_2(T,\|\cdot\|_2)\). The width of every set in Lecture 3 and Lecture 13 could, in principle, be computed by exhibiting an admissible sequence and a matching tree.
Comparison for sub-Gaussian processes. If \((X_t)\) is sub-Gaussian with respect to the canonical metric of a Gaussian process \((Y_t)\) on the same index set, then \[
\mathbb E\sup_tX_t\leq C\gamma_2(T,d)\leq C'\,\mathbb E\sup_tY_t .
\] Thus every sub-Gaussian process is dominated by a Gaussian process with the same increments, a statement that has no direct proof and is the main practical use of the theorem. Lecture 19 applies it to random matrices with sub-Gaussian rows.
The gap between Sudakov and Dudley is closed. For Gaussian processes the expected supremum is neither the largest rectangle under the entropy curve nor the area under it. It is \(\gamma_2\), a quantity that sees the entropy of each region of \(T\) at each scale, and it coincides with the rectangle for some sets, with the area for others, and with neither in general.

title: Lecture 18: Generic Chaining
text:
5 Where we go next
The next lecture completes the proof of the majorizing measure theorem with the tree construction and the sharpened Sudakov lemma from the handwritten notes, and then turns the theorem into a tool: the matrix deviation inequality, which controls \(\sup_{x\in T}\big|\|Ax\|_2-\sqrt m\|x\|_2\big|\) for a matrix \(A\) with independent sub-Gaussian rows by the Gaussian width of \(T\). That inequality is what the covariance estimation problem of Lecture 9 was missing.

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
text: Sudakov’s minoration, proved in Lecture 12, bounds the expected supremum of a Gaussian process from below by the metric entropy of its index set at a single scale. This lecture proves the matching upper bound, Dudley’s inequality, which integrates the entropy over all scales. The proof is chaining, a multiscale version of the net arguments used since Lecture 8, and it applies to a class of processes much wider than Gaussian ones: all that is needed is a sub-Gaussian bound on increments. The lecture ends with examples showing where the entropy integral is sharp and where it is not. The gap it leaves is the subject of the generic chaining lectures.

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
text:
1 Sub-Gaussian processes

Definition 1 (Sub-Gaussian process) Let \((T,d)\) be a metric space. A centered process \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(d\) if \[
\|X_t-X_s\|_{\psi_2}\leq d(t,s)
\qquad\text{for all }s,t\in T .
\]

If the increments satisfy \(\|X_t-X_s\|_{\psi_2}\leq Kd(t,s)\) instead, the process is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(Kd\), and every bound below scales by \(K\). The metric need not be the canonical one; any metric dominating the \(\psi_2\) distance will do, at the cost of larger covering numbers.






NoteExamples





Gaussian processes. If \((X_t)\) is centered Gaussian with canonical metric \(d\), then \(X_t-X_s\sim N(0,d(t,s)^2)\), and the sub-Gaussian–\(\psi_2\) comparison of Lecture 5 gives \(\|X_t-X_s\|_{\psi_2}\leq2d(t,s)\). So a Gaussian process is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(2d\).
Rademacher processes. Let \(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n\) be independent random signs and \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). The process \(X_t=\sum_i\varepsilon_it_i\) has increments \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i(t_i-s_i)\), which are \(\|t-s\|_2^2\)-subgaussian by the Pythagorean theorem of Lecture 5, so the process is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(2\|t-s\|_2\). Its expected supremum is the Rademacher complexity of \(T\), mentioned in Lecture 3.
Empirical processes. Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be i.i.d. in a space \(\mathcal Y\) and let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions \(f:\mathcal Y\to[-1,1]\). The process \[
X_f:=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(f(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y_i)\big)
\] has increments that are sums of independent bounded variables, so by Hoeffding’s lemma of Lecture 4 it is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(C\|f-g\|_\infty\). Sharper metrics, such as the \(L^2\) distance under the law of \(Y_1\), are available with more work.



Two facts about finitely many sub-Gaussian variables drive the proof.

Lemma 1 (Maximum of finitely many sub-Gaussian variables) Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) be random variables with \(\|Y_i\|_{\psi_2}\leq L\), \(N\geq2\). Then for every \(u\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\max_{i\leq N}|Y_i|\geq L\big(\sqrt{\log N}+u\big)\Big\}\leq2e^{-u^2},
\qquad
\mathbb E\max_{i\leq N}|Y_i|\leq CL\sqrt{\log N}.
\]







NoteProof





By the Markov direction of the equivalence theorem of Lecture 5, \(\mathbb P\{|Y_i|\geq s\}\leq2e^{-s^2/L^2}\). A union bound at \(s=L(\sqrt{\log N}+u)\) gives, using \((\sqrt{\log N}+u)^2\geq\log N+u^2\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\max_i|Y_i|\geq s\Big\}\leq2Ne^{-\log N-u^2}=2e^{-u^2}.
\] For the expectation, integrate the tail: \(\mathbb E\max_i|Y_i|\leq L\sqrt{\log N}+L\int_0^\infty2e^{-u^2}\,du\leq L(\sqrt{\log N}+\sqrt\pi)\), and \(\sqrt\pi\leq3\sqrt{\log2}\leq3\sqrt{\log N}\).

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
text:
2 Dudley’s inequality
For a metric space \((T,d)\) recall the covering number \(N(T,d,\varepsilon)\) from Lecture 1, with centers in \(T\). It equals \(1\) once \(\varepsilon\geq\operatorname{diam}(T)\), so the integrals below are really over \([0,\operatorname{diam}(T)]\).

Theorem 1 (Dudley’s inequality) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) be a centered process, sub-Gaussian with respect to a metric \(d\) for which \((T,d)\) is separable. Then \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq C\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon ,
\] and for every \(u\geq0\), with probability at least \(1-2e^{-u^2}\), \[
\sup_{s,t\in T}|X_t-X_s|\leq C\Big[\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon+u\operatorname{diam}(T)\Big].
\]

The proof is a walk. Fix a base point \(t_0\) and, for each \(t\), a chain of approximations \(\pi_{k_0}(t)=t_0,\pi_{k_0+1}(t),\pi_{k_0+2}(t),\ldots\) drawn from nets of \(T\) at the dyadic scales \(2^{-k}\), converging to \(t\). The increment \(X_t-X_{t_0}\) is the sum of the increments along the chain. At scale \(k\) there are only \(N(T,d,2^{-k})^2\) possible links, each an increment of \(\psi_2\) norm at most \(2^{-k+2}\), so a union bound controls all links at that scale by \(2^{-k}\sqrt{\log N(T,d,2^{-k})}\), and summing over \(k\) gives a Riemann sum for the entropy integral. The single-scale net argument of Lecture 8 stopped after one step and could not control the remainder \(X_t-X_{\pi(t)}\) uniformly in \(t\); chaining simply keeps going.






NoteProof





Step 0: reductions. It suffices to treat finite \(T\). For separable \((T,d)\) and the supremum convention of Lecture 10, applied along a countable dense subset, \(\sup_TX\) is the increasing limit of suprema over finite subsets \(T'\subseteq T\), so the expectation bound follows by monotone convergence and the tail bound by passing to the limit in the events. The covering numbers of a subset are controlled by those of \(T\): covering \(T\) by \(N(T,d,\varepsilon/2)\) balls of radius \(\varepsilon/2\) and picking a point of \(T'\) in each ball that meets \(T'\) gives \(N(T',d,\varepsilon)\leq N(T,d,\varepsilon/2)\), and the change of variable \(\varepsilon\mapsto\varepsilon/2\) costs a factor \(2\) in the integral.
So let \(T\) be finite, with \(D:=\operatorname{diam}(T)\). Let \(k_0\) be the integer with \(2^{-k_0-1}<D\leq2^{-k_0}\), and for \(k\geq k_0\) let \(T_k\subseteq T\) be a \(2^{-k}\)-net of \(T\) with \(|T_k|=N_k:=N(T,d,2^{-k})\). We may take \(T_{k_0}=\{t_0\}\), and since \(T\) is finite, \(T_k=T\) for all large \(k\). For \(t\in T\) let \(\pi_k(t)\in T_k\) be a nearest point, so \(d(t,\pi_k(t))\leq2^{-k}\) and \(\pi_k(t)=t\) for large \(k\).
Step 1: the chain. For every \(t\in T\), \[
X_t-X_{t_0}=\sum_{k>k_0}\big(X_{\pi_k(t)}-X_{\pi_{k-1}(t)}\big),
\] a finite sum since the terms vanish once \(\pi_k(t)=t\). Each link joins two points at distance \[
d\big(\pi_k(t),\pi_{k-1}(t)\big)\leq d(\pi_k(t),t)+d(t,\pi_{k-1}(t))\leq2^{-k}+2^{-k+1}\leq2^{-k+2},
\] so \(\|X_{\pi_k(t)}-X_{\pi_{k-1}(t)}\|_{\psi_2}\leq2^{-k+2}\). As \(t\) ranges over \(T\), the pair \((\pi_k(t),\pi_{k-1}(t))\) ranges over a set of at most \(N_kN_{k-1}\leq N_k^2\) pairs.
Step 2: each scale. Apply Lemma 1 at scale \(k\) to the at most \(N_k^2\) variables \(X_a-X_b\), \((a,b)\) a possible link, with \(L=2^{-k+2}\). For \(u_k\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{t\in T}\big|X_{\pi_k(t)}-X_{\pi_{k-1}(t)}\big|\geq2^{-k+2}\big(\sqrt{2\log N_k}+u_k\big)\Big\}\leq2e^{-u_k^2},
\] when \(N_k\geq2\); when \(N_k=1\) the link is trivial and the event is empty.
Step 3: summing the scales. Take \(u_k:=u+\sqrt{k-k_0}\). The failure probabilities sum to at most \(\sum_{j\geq1}2e^{-(u+\sqrt j)^2}\leq2e^{-u^2}\sum_{j\geq1}e^{-j}\leq2e^{-u^2}\). On the complementary event, for every \(t\), \[
|X_t-X_{t_0}|\leq\sum_{k>k_0}2^{-k+2}\Big(\sqrt{2\log N_k}+u+\sqrt{k-k_0}\Big)
\leq4\sqrt2\sum_{k>k_0}2^{-k}\sqrt{\log N_k}+4\cdot2^{-k_0}\big(u+2\big),
\] using \(\sum_{j\geq1}2^{-j}\sqrt j\leq2\). Since \(2^{-k_0}<2D\), the last term is at most \(8D(u+2)\), and \(16D\leq16\cdot2\int_0^{D/2}d\varepsilon\) can be absorbed into the entropy integral because \(\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)\geq\log2\) for \(\varepsilon<D/2\) (two points at distance \(D\) cannot share a ball of radius less than \(D/2\)). Applying the bound to \(s\) and \(t\) and using the triangle inequality gives the tail bound with the dyadic sum in place of the integral.
Step 4: from the sum to the integral. For each \(k\), \(2^{-k}=2\int_{2^{-k-1}}^{2^{-k}}d\varepsilon\), and on that interval \(N(T,d,\varepsilon)\geq N_k\) since \(\varepsilon\leq2^{-k}\). Hence \[
\sum_{k>k_0}2^{-k}\sqrt{\log N_k}\leq2\sum_{k>k_0}\int_{2^{-k-1}}^{2^{-k}}\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon\leq2\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon .
\]
Step 5: the expectation. Since \(\mathbb EX_{t_0}=0\), \(\mathbb E\sup_tX_t=\mathbb E\sup_t(X_t-X_{t_0})\leq\mathbb E\sup_t|X_t-X_{t_0}|\), and integrating the tail bound over \(u\) gives the claim.



The hypothesis \(\mathbb EX_t=0\) is used only in the last step; the tail bound on \(\sup|X_t-X_s|\) needs no centering. For a Gaussian process the metric is the canonical one up to the factor \(2\), and the theorem says \[
c\,\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}
\leq\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t
\leq C\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon ,
\] the left side being Sudakov’s minoration. The lower bound is the largest rectangle under the graph of \(\varepsilon\mapsto\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\) and the upper bound is the area under it. When the graph is roughly a hyperbola \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) the two differ by a logarithm, and the examples below show that the gap is real.

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
section: 3 Where the entropy integral is sharp
text:
3 Where the entropy integral is sharp
The Euclidean ball. For \(T=B_2^n\) with the Gaussian width process, the volumetric bound of Lecture 1 gives \(N(T,\varepsilon)\leq(3/\varepsilon)^n\) for \(\varepsilon\leq1\), so \[
\int_0^2\sqrt{\log N(T,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon\leq\sqrt n\int_0^1\sqrt{\log(3/\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon+\sqrt{\log2}\leq C\sqrt n ,
\] the integral converging because \(\sqrt{\log(3/\varepsilon)}\) is integrable at \(0\). Since \(w(B_2^n)=\mathbb E\|g\|_2\asymp\sqrt n\), Dudley’s bound is sharp up to the constant.
Sparse vectors. For \(T=U_s\), the \(s\)-sparse vectors in the unit ball, \(U_s\) is a union of \(\binom ns\) balls of dimension \(s\), so \(N(U_s,\varepsilon)\leq\binom ns(3/\varepsilon)^s\leq(en/s)^s(3/\varepsilon)^s\) and \[
\int_0^2\sqrt{\log N(U_s,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon
\leq\int_0^1\Big(\sqrt{s\log(en/s)}+\sqrt{s\log(3/\varepsilon)}\Big)d\varepsilon+\sqrt{\log2}
\leq C\sqrt{s\log(en/s)} .
\] This matches the width computed in Lecture 13, so Dudley is sharp here too, and it recovers the sparse-width bound of Exercise Sheet 3 by a different route. The subadditivity of \(\sqrt{a+b}\leq\sqrt a+\sqrt b\) is what lets the two sources of entropy, the choice of support and the ball within it, be integrated separately.






NoteThe spherical \(p\)-spin process





Let \(G\) be a Gaussian tensor with independent \(N(0,1)\) entries indexed by \(\{1,\ldots,d\}^p\), and for \(u\in S^{d-1}\) let \(X_u:=\langle G,u^{\otimes p}\rangle\). By the tensor identity of Lecture 15, \(\mathbb EX_uX_v=\langle u,v\rangle^p\), so \(\operatorname{Var}X_u=1\) and \[
d(u,v)^2=2\big(1-\langle u,v\rangle^p\big).
\] For \(p=2\), \(X_u=\langle Gu,u\rangle\) is a quadratic form and \(\sup_uX_u\) is the largest eigenvalue of \((G+G^{\mathsf T})/2\), of order \(\sqrt d\). For larger \(p\) the metric changes character: \(d(u,v)\leq\varepsilon\) forces \(\langle u,v\rangle^p\geq1-\varepsilon^2/2\), hence \(\|u-v\|_2\lesssim\varepsilon/\sqrt p\), so \(N(T,d,\varepsilon)\approx N(S^{d-1},\varepsilon/\sqrt p)\) and the entropy integral is \[
\int_0^{\sqrt2}\sqrt{d\log(C\sqrt p/\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon\asymp\sqrt{d\log p}
\qquad(p\geq2).
\] Sudakov at \(\varepsilon=1\) gives the same order from below, since a \(1\)-separated set in \(d\) is a \(\sqrt{(2\log2)/p}\)-separated set on the sphere, and a maximal such subset of a hemisphere, which avoids antipodal pairs, has \(p^{cd}\) points by the volume argument of Lecture 1. So \(\mathbb E\sup_uX_u\asymp\sqrt{d\log p}\) for \(2\leq p\leq e^d\), both bounds are sharp, and the supremum genuinely grows with \(p\) at fixed \(d\): the process decorrelates faster on the sphere as \(p\) grows, and more of the \(\sqrt{2\log(\text{number of points})}\) behavior of independent Gaussians appears.

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
text:
4 Where it is not






NoteTalagrand’s example





Let \(T=\{t_n:n\geq1\}\subseteq\ell^2\) with \(t_n=e_n/\sqrt{1+\log n}\), and let \(X_{t}=g(t)\) be the isonormal process of Lecture 10 restricted to \(T\). Then \(X_{t_n}=Z_n/\sqrt{1+\log n}\) for i.i.d. standard Gaussians \(Z_n\).
The supremum is finite. For \(s>\sqrt2\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_nX_{t_n}\geq s\Big\}\leq\sum_{n\geq1}\mathbb P\{Z_n\geq s\sqrt{1+\log n}\}
\leq\sum_{n\geq1}e^{-s^2(1+\log n)/2}=e^{-s^2/2}\sum_{n\geq1}n^{-s^2/2}<\infty ,
\] and the sum decays in \(s\) fast enough that \(\mathbb E\sup_nX_{t_n}<\infty\).
The entropy integral is infinite. For \(m<n\), \[
d(t_m,t_n)^2=\|t_m-t_n\|_2^2=\frac1{1+\log m}+\frac1{1+\log n}\geq\frac2{1+\log n},
\] so the first \(n\) points are \(\varepsilon\)-separated as long as \(2/(1+\log n)\geq\varepsilon^2\), that is \(n\leq e^{2/\varepsilon^2-1}\). Hence \(\log N(T,d,\varepsilon/2)\geq2/\varepsilon^2-1\), and \(\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)}\gtrsim1/\varepsilon\) for small \(\varepsilon\), which is not integrable at \(0\).
The covering numbers grow like \(\exp(c/\varepsilon^2)\), which is the critical rate: a hair slower and Dudley converges, as for the Euclidean ball. What Dudley cannot see is that the points that force the large covering numbers, the \(t_n\) with \(n\) large, contribute almost nothing to the supremum because their variances \(1/(1+\log n)\) are tiny. Entropy counts points; it does not weigh them.



A second, more elementary failure is worth recording. For \(T=B_1^n\) the width is \(\mathbb E\|g\|_\infty\asymp\sqrt{\log n}\), while the covering numbers of Lecture 2 give an entropy integral of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\cdot\log n\) once the scales below \(n^{-1/2}\) are included. Dudley’s bound is off by a logarithm. Sudakov, on the other hand, is sharp for \(B_1^n\), so the truth sits at the lower bound. For the sparse vectors it sat at the upper bound. Neither inequality can be the whole story.

title: Lecture 16: Dudley’s Entropy Integral
text:
5 Where we go next
Dudley’s inequality is a tool of enormous reach. The next lecture applies it to empirical processes, proving a uniform law of large numbers over a class of Lipschitz functions and the continuity of Brownian motion. After that, Talagrand’s generic chaining closes the gap exposed in this lecture: it replaces the entropy integral, which uses the same net at every point of \(T\), by a functional that lets the nets adapt to the geometry, and for Gaussian processes it is sharp in both directions.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text: The last four lectures used Gaussian vectors to study suprema of random functions. This lecture uses them for something different: to solve, or nearly solve, a hard combinatorial optimization problem. The problem is to maximize a quadratic form over the vertices of the discrete cube \(\{-1,1\}^n\). A union bound over \(2^n\) points is useless here, and the tools are instead convex relaxation, which replaces the cube by a convex set of matrices, and randomized rounding, which uses a Gaussian vector to map a point of the convex set back to the cube. The analysis of the rounding step is a single identity about the signs of two correlated Gaussians, and the identity is exactly what Grothendieck’s inequality, in the next lecture, is built around.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
1 Quadratic optimization over the cube
Let \(A\) be a symmetric \(n\times n\) real matrix. The problem is \[
\mathrm{INT}(A):=\max\Big\{\sum_{i,j=1}^nA_{ij}x_ix_j:\ x\in\{-1,1\}^n\Big\}
=\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\langle Ax,x\rangle .
\] The feasible set has \(2^n\) points, and exhaustive search is exponential. No essentially faster exact method is expected to exist, because the problem is NP-hard. The standard witness to its hardness is the maximum cut problem for graphs.

Definition 1 (Maximum cut) Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple undirected graph on \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with adjacency matrix \(A\), so \(A_{ij}=1\) if \(\{i,j\}\in E\) and \(A_{ij}=0\) otherwise. A partition of \(V\) into two sets is encoded by a vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\), and its cut is the number of edges joining the two sets, \[
\mathrm{CUT}(G,x):=\#\big\{\{i,j\}\in E:\ x_i\neq x_j\big\}
=\frac14\sum_{i,j=1}^nA_{ij}(1-x_ix_j).
\] The maximum cut is \(\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G):=\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\).

The formula for \(\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\) holds because \(1-x_ix_j\) is \(2\) when \(x_i\neq x_j\) and \(0\) otherwise, and each edge is counted twice in the double sum. Expanding, \(\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)=\frac12|E|-\frac14\langle Ax,x\rangle\), so the maximum cut is the problem \(\mathrm{INT}(-A)\) up to an additive constant. Computing \(\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G)\) exactly is NP-hard, which we take as known.
Since exact solutions are out of reach, the goal is an approximation algorithm: an efficient procedure that produces a cut of size at least \(\alpha\cdot\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G)\) for some constant \(\alpha<1\), on every graph. The first such algorithm needs no ideas at all.

Proposition 1 (A random cut) Let \(x\) be uniformly distributed on \(\{-1,1\}^n\). Then \[
\mathbb E\,\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)=\frac12|E|\geq\frac12\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G).
\]







NoteProof





The coordinates of \(x\) are independent symmetric signs, so \(\mathbb Ex_ix_j=0\) for \(i\neq j\), and \(A_{ii}=0\) because the graph has no loops. Taking expectations in the formula for \(\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\) leaves \(\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}=\frac12|E|\). The inequality is \(\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G)\leq|E|\).



A random partition cuts half the edges on average, so it is a \(\frac12\)-approximation in expectation. Repeating the experiment a few times and keeping the best cut gives a \((\frac12-\varepsilon)\)-approximation with high probability. Doing better requires looking at the graph.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
2 The semidefinite relaxation
The idea of relaxation is to enlarge the feasible set to a convex one over which the maximum can be computed, and then to argue that the enlargement does not increase the maximum by much. For \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\), the natural enlargement replaces each sign \(x_i\in\{-1,1\}\), a unit vector in \(\mathbb R^1\), by a unit vector \(X_i\) in \(\mathbb R^n\): \[
\mathrm{SDP}(A):=\max\Big\{\sum_{i,j=1}^nA_{ij}\langle X_i,X_j\rangle:\ X_1,\ldots,X_n\in S^{n-1}\Big\}.
\] Taking \(X_i=x_ie_1\) shows \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\leq\mathrm{SDP}(A)\). The name comes from a reformulation in terms of the Gram matrix of the \(X_i\).

Lemma 1 (Gram matrices of unit vectors) An \(n\times n\) matrix \(X\) is the Gram matrix \(X_{ij}=\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) of some unit vectors \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(X\) is positive semidefinite with \(X_{ii}=1\) for every \(i\). The vectors can be read off from \(X\) as the columns of \(X^{1/2}\).







NoteProof





If \(X_{ij}=\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) then \(X=M^{\mathsf T}M\) with \(M\) the matrix whose columns are the \(X_i\), so \(\langle Xa,a\rangle=\|Ma\|_2^2\geq0\), and \(X_{ii}=\|X_i\|_2^2=1\). Conversely, if \(X\succeq0\) with unit diagonal, let \(M=X^{1/2}\) be the positive semidefinite square root. Then \(X=M^{\mathsf T}M\), so \(X_{ij}\) is the inner product of the \(i\)-th and \(j\)-th columns of \(M\), and these columns are unit vectors because \(X_{ii}=1\).



Writing \(\langle A,X\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}X)=\sum_{ij}A_{ij}X_{ij}\) for the trace inner product on matrices, the lemma gives \[
\mathrm{SDP}(A)=\max\big\{\langle A,X\rangle:\ X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\text{ for all }i\big\}.
\] This is a maximization of a linear function over the intersection of the convex cone of positive semidefinite matrices with an affine subspace, which is a convex set. In particular the maximum exists, since the feasible set is compact.

Definition 2 (Semidefinite program) A semidefinite program is an optimization problem of the form \[
\text{maximize }\langle A,X\rangle\quad\text{subject to}\quad X\succeq0,\ \ \langle B_k,X\rangle=b_k\ \ (k=1,\ldots,m),
\] where \(A,B_1,\ldots,B_m\) are given symmetric matrices and \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\) are given reals.

The relaxation \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) is the case \(B_k=e_ke_k^{\mathsf T}\), \(b_k=1\). Semidefinite programs are convex programs, and they can be solved to any prescribed accuracy in time polynomial in \(n\) and in the number of accuracy digits, for instance by interior point methods. We treat this as a black box: the value \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) and a maximizing configuration \((X_i)\) are available.
Two things remain. First, how much larger than \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\) can \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) be? Second, given a maximizing configuration of unit vectors, how does one produce a point of the cube? The second question is answered by a Gaussian vector, and its analysis answers the first.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
3 Rounding by a random hyperplane
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in S^{n-1}\) be given. Choose \(g\sim N(0,I_n)\) and set \[
x_i:=\operatorname{sgn}\langle X_i,g\rangle,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n .
\] Geometrically, the hyperplane \(g^\perp\) splits the sphere into two hemispheres, and \(x_i\) records which hemisphere contains \(X_i\). Two vectors that are close on the sphere are likely to land on the same side, so the rounding respects the geometry of the configuration. The following identity quantifies this.

Lemma 2 (Grothendieck’s identity) Let \(g\sim N(0,I_n)\) and let \(u,v\in S^{n-1}\). Then \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{sgn}\langle g,u\rangle\operatorname{sgn}\langle g,v\rangle
=\frac2\pi\arcsin\langle u,v\rangle .
\]







NoteProof





Let \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) be the angle between \(u\) and \(v\), so \(\langle u,v\rangle=\cos\theta\). By the rotation invariance of \(g\) (Lecture 10) we may assume \(u=e_1\) and \(v=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2\). Then \(\langle g,u\rangle=g_1\) and \(\langle g,v\rangle=g_1\cos\theta+g_2\sin\theta\) depend only on the planar vector \((g_1,g_2)\), which is rotation invariant in \(\mathbb R^2\), so its direction is uniform on the circle.
The signs of \(\langle g,u\rangle\) and \(\langle g,v\rangle\) differ exactly when \((g_1,g_2)\) lies on opposite sides of the two lines \(u^\perp\) and \(v^\perp\) through the origin. These lines make an angle \(\theta\), and they divide the plane into four sectors, of which the two where the signs differ have angles \(\theta\) and \(\theta\). Hence \[
\mathbb P\big\{\operatorname{sgn}\langle g,u\rangle\neq\operatorname{sgn}\langle g,v\rangle\big\}=\frac{2\theta}{2\pi}=\frac\theta\pi ,
\] and the product of the signs has expectation \(1-2\theta/\pi=\frac2\pi\big(\frac\pi2-\theta\big)=\frac2\pi\arcsin(\cos\theta)\). The event \(\langle g,u\rangle=0\) has probability zero and does not affect the computation.



Compare the identity \(\mathbb E\langle g,u\rangle\langle g,v\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\) of Lecture 10. Taking signs replaces the linear function \(t\mapsto t\) by the nonlinear \(t\mapsto\frac2\pi\arcsin t\), which agrees with the linear function at \(t=\pm1\), lies below it on \((0,1)\), and above it on \((-1,0)\). Everything in the analysis of rounding, and in Grothendieck’s inequality, is about the gap between these two functions.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
4 The Goemans–Williamson algorithm
For the maximum cut problem, the relaxation is \[
\mathrm{SDP}(G):=\max\Big\{\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\big(1-\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\big):\ X_i\in S^{n-1}\Big\}
\geq\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G),
\] which is a semidefinite program by Lemma 1. The algorithm is: solve the relaxation, then round the solution by a random hyperplane.
The analysis needs one numerical fact. Define \[
\alpha:=\min_{0<\theta\leq\pi}\frac2\pi\cdot\frac\theta{1-\cos\theta}.
\] The function being minimized tends to \(+\infty\) as \(\theta\downarrow0\), since \(1-\cos\theta\sim\theta^2/2\), and equals \(1\) at \(\theta=\pi\), so the minimum exists and is positive. It is attained at the unique solution of \(1-\cos\theta=\theta\sin\theta\) in \((0,\pi)\), which is \(\theta\approx2.33\), and its value is \[
\alpha\approx0.8786 .
\] Substituting \(t=\cos\theta\), the definition of \(\alpha\) says precisely that \[
\frac2\pi\arccos t\geq\alpha(1-t)
\qquad\text{for all }t\in[-1,1] .
\tag{1}\]

Theorem 1 (Goemans–Williamson) Let \(G\) be a graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), let \((X_i)\) be a maximizer of \(\mathrm{SDP}(G)\), and let \(x=(\operatorname{sgn}\langle X_i,g\rangle)_i\) be its rounding by a random hyperplane. Then \[
\mathbb E\,\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\geq\alpha\cdot\mathrm{SDP}(G)\geq\alpha\cdot\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G),
\qquad\alpha\approx0.8786 .
\]







NoteProof





By the cut formula, linearity of expectation, and Lemma 2, \[
\mathbb E\,\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)=\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\big(1-\mathbb Ex_ix_j\big)
=\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\Big(1-\frac2\pi\arcsin\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\Big)
=\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\,\frac2\pi\arccos\langle X_i,X_j\rangle .
\] Every \(A_{ij}\) is nonnegative, so Equation 1 may be applied term by term: \[
\mathbb E\,\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\geq\alpha\cdot\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\big(1-\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\big)=\alpha\cdot\mathrm{SDP}(G).
\] The second inequality is \(\mathrm{SDP}(G)\geq\mathrm{MAX\text{-}CUT}(G)\).



Several remarks.
The bound is in expectation, but that is enough. The random variable \(\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\) takes values in \([0,|E|]\), so \(\mathbb P\{\mathrm{CUT}(G,x)\geq(\alpha-\varepsilon)\mathrm{SDP}(G)\}\geq c\varepsilon\) for a constant \(c\) depending on \(|E|/\mathrm{SDP}(G)\leq2\), by the reverse Markov inequality. Repeating the rounding \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\eta))\) times and keeping the best cut therefore gives an \((\alpha-\varepsilon)\)-approximation with probability at least \(1-\eta\). The rounding can also be derandomized, but the random version is the natural one.
Where the constant comes from. The relaxation loses nothing on the constraint side, since the cube is contained in the feasible set. All of the loss is in the rounding step, and it is measured by the ratio of \(\frac2\pi\arccos t\) to \(1-t\) in Equation 1. The worst case is an edge whose endpoints make angle \(\theta\approx2.33\) in the relaxed solution, for which the hyperplane cuts the edge with probability \(\theta/\pi\approx0.74\) while the relaxation counts it with weight \((1-\cos\theta)/2\approx0.85\).
The constant is believed optimal. Håstad proved that no polynomial time algorithm achieves a ratio above \(16/17\approx0.941\) unless P equals NP, and Khot, Kindler, Mossel and O’Donnell (Khot et al. 2007) showed that under the Unique Games Conjecture no polynomial time algorithm achieves a ratio above \(\alpha\) itself. The random hyperplane is then the best possible rounding of the best possible relaxation. The algorithm is due to Goemans and Williamson (Goemans and Williamson 1995).

Khot, Subhash, Guy Kindler, Elchanan Mossel, and Ryan O’Donnell. 2007. “Optimal Inapproximability Results for MAX-CUT and Other 2-Variable CSPs?” SIAM Journal on Computing 37 (1): 319–57. https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539705447372.

Goemans, Michel X., and David P. Williamson. 1995. “Improved Approximation Algorithms for Maximum Cut and Satisfiability Problems Using Semidefinite Programming.” Journal of the ACM 42 (6): 1115–45. https://doi.org/10.1145/227683.227684.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
5 Beyond max-cut
The argument used two features of the cut objective: the coefficients \(A_{ij}\) are nonnegative, and the objective involves \(1-\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) rather than \(\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) alone. Both fail for the general problem \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\). For a symmetric \(A\) with entries of both signs, rounding a maximizer \((X_i)\) of \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) gives \[
\mathbb E\langle Ax,x\rangle=\frac2\pi\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\arcsin\langle X_i,X_j\rangle ,
\] and there is no termwise inequality relating \(\arcsin\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) to \(\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) that respects the signs of the coefficients. If the nonlinearity were absent, that is, if \(\arcsin t\) could be replaced by \(t\), we would have \(\mathbb E\langle Ax,x\rangle=\frac2\pi\mathrm{SDP}(A)\), and hence \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\geq\frac2\pi\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) for every \(A\).
Whether some inequality of this form holds, \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\leq K\cdot\mathrm{INT}(A)\) with a constant \(K\) independent of \(A\) and \(n\), is not at all obvious. The statement that it does is Grothendieck’s inequality, and the next lecture proves it by a device that removes the nonlinearity: the vectors \(X_i\) are replaced by vectors \(\Phi(X_i)\) in a larger Hilbert space, chosen so that the arcsine of their inner products is a linear function of the original inner products. The rounding then becomes exact, and the Gaussian vector used to round is the isonormal process of Lecture 10 on the larger space.
The same question arises for the bilinear problem \[
\max\Big\{\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}x_iy_j:\ x\in\{-1,1\}^m,\ y\in\{-1,1\}^n\Big\},
\] whose value is the cut norm of \(A\), a quantity that governs the regularity of graphs and the approximation of dense combinatorial problems. Its semidefinite relaxation, over unit vectors \(X_i\) and \(Y_j\), is the setting in which Grothendieck’s inequality is usually stated.

title: Lecture 14: Semidefinite Relaxations and Max-Cut
text:
6 Where we go next
The next lecture states Grothendieck’s inequality, deduces from it that the bilinear relaxation is tight up to the constant \(K\), explains why the symmetric problem is genuinely harder, and proves the inequality with \(K\leq\pi/(2\log(1+\sqrt2))\approx1.78\) by Krivine’s kernel-trick argument.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text: Lecture 11 reduced the study of the supremum of a Gaussian process to the study of its mean. This lecture develops the main tool for the mean. The idea is to compare two Gaussian processes on the same index set: if the increments of \(X\) are smaller than those of \(Y\) in the canonical metric, then \(\mathbb E\sup X\leq\mathbb E\sup Y\). The proof is Stein’s lemma along an interpolation between the two covariances, in the same way that the concentration inequality was Stein’s lemma along an interpolation between a Gaussian vector and an independent copy. The two applications are the norm of a Gaussian random matrix, where comparison with a process that can be computed exactly gives the sharp bound \(\sqrt m+\sqrt n\), and Sudakov’s minoration, whose proof Lecture 3 postponed to this point.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
1 Gaussian interpolation
Let \(X\sim N(0,\Sigma^X)\) and \(Y\sim N(0,\Sigma^Y)\) be independent Gaussian vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(u\in[0,1]\) set \[
Z(u):=\sqrt u\,X+\sqrt{1-u}\,Y .
\] Then \(Z(u)\sim N\big(0,\,u\Sigma^X+(1-u)\Sigma^Y\big)\): the covariance interpolates linearly between \(\Sigma^Y\) at \(u=0\) and \(\Sigma^X\) at \(u=1\). The question is how \(\mathbb Ef(Z(u))\) varies along the path.

Lemma 1 (Gaussian interpolation) Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\) with bounded first and second derivatives. Then for \(0<u<1\), \[
\frac d{du}\mathbb Ef(Z(u))
=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^n\big(\Sigma^X_{ij}-\Sigma^Y_{ij}\big)\,\mathbb E\,\partial_{ij}f(Z(u)).
\]







NoteProof





By the chain rule and differentiation under the expectation, which the bounded gradient justifies, \[
\frac d{du}\mathbb Ef(Z(u))
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\Big[\partial_if(Z(u))\Big(\frac{X_i}{2\sqrt u}-\frac{Y_i}{2\sqrt{1-u}}\Big)\Big].
\] Consider the terms containing \(X_i\). Condition on \(Y\); then \(x\mapsto\partial_if(\sqrt u\,x+\sqrt{1-u}\,Y)\) is Lipschitz with gradient \(\sqrt u\,\nabla\partial_if(Z(u))\), and the multivariate Stein lemma of Lecture 10 gives \[
\mathbb E\big[X_i\,\partial_if(Z(u))\,\big|\,Y\big]
=\sqrt u\sum_{j=1}^n\Sigma^X_{ij}\,\mathbb E\big[\partial_{ij}f(Z(u))\,\big|\,Y\big].
\] Taking expectations and summing over \(i\), the \(X\) terms contribute \(\frac12\sum_{ij}\Sigma^X_{ij}\mathbb E\partial_{ij}f(Z(u))\). The \(Y\) terms are handled in the same way, conditioning on \(X\), and contribute \(-\frac12\sum_{ij}\Sigma^Y_{ij}\mathbb E\partial_{ij}f(Z(u))\).



Everything that follows is a choice of \(f\) for which the sign of the right side can be read off from the covariances.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
2 Slepian’s inequality

Lemma 2 (Slepian’s lemma) Let \(X\sim N(0,\Sigma^X)\) and \(Y\sim N(0,\Sigma^Y)\) in \(\mathbb R^n\) with \[
\Sigma^X_{ii}=\Sigma^Y_{ii}\quad\text{for all }i,
\qquad
\Sigma^X_{ij}\geq\Sigma^Y_{ij}\quad\text{for all }i\neq j .
\] Let \(f\) be \(C^2\) with bounded derivatives and \(\partial_{ij}f\geq0\) for all \(i\neq j\). Then \(\mathbb Ef(X)\geq\mathbb Ef(Y)\).







NoteProof





We may take \(X\) and \(Y\) independent, since the conclusion involves only their individual laws. In Lemma 1 the diagonal terms vanish because \(\Sigma^X_{ii}=\Sigma^Y_{ii}\), and each off-diagonal term is a product of the nonnegative quantities \(\Sigma^X_{ij}-\Sigma^Y_{ij}\) and \(\mathbb E\partial_{ij}f(Z(u))\). So \(u\mapsto\mathbb Ef(Z(u))\) is nondecreasing on \([0,1]\), and \(\mathbb Ef(Y)=\mathbb Ef(Z(0))\leq\mathbb Ef(Z(1))=\mathbb Ef(X)\).



In the language of processes, the hypotheses say that \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same variances and \(X\) has the smaller increments: \[
\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2=\Sigma^X_{ii}+\Sigma^X_{jj}-2\Sigma^X_{ij}
\leq\Sigma^Y_{ii}+\Sigma^Y_{jj}-2\Sigma^Y_{ij}=\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2 .
\] The process with smaller increments is the more correlated one, and its maximum should be smaller, because its coordinates cannot spread out as far. Slepian’s inequality makes this precise at the level of tails.

Theorem 1 (Slepian’s inequality) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) and \((Y_t)_{t\in T}\) be centered Gaussian processes on a set \(T\) whose canonical metric spaces are separable, and suppose that for all \(s,t\in T\), \[
\mathbb EX_t^2=\mathbb EY_t^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb E(X_t-X_s)^2\leq\mathbb E(Y_t-Y_s)^2 .
\] Then for every \(\tau\in\mathbb R\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{t\in T}X_t>\tau\Big\}\leq\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{t\in T}Y_t>\tau\Big\},
\] and consequently \(\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\) whenever either side is finite.







NoteProof





Finite \(T\). Let \(T=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Fix \(\tau\) and let \(h:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\) be \(C^2\), nonincreasing, with bounded derivatives, equal to \(1\) on \((-\infty,\tau]\) and to \(0\) on \([\tau+\varepsilon,\infty)\). Set \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^nh(x_i)\). For \(i\neq j\), \[
\partial_{ij}f(x)=h'(x_i)h'(x_j)\prod_{k\neq i,j}h(x_k)\geq0,
\] since \(h'\leq0\) and \(h\geq0\). By Lemma 2, \(\mathbb Ef(X)\geq\mathbb Ef(Y)\). Now \(\mathbb 1\{\max_ix_i\leq\tau\}\leq f(x)\leq\mathbb 1\{\max_ix_i\leq\tau+\varepsilon\}\), so \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\max_iX_i\leq\tau+\varepsilon\Big\}\geq\mathbb Ef(X)\geq\mathbb Ef(Y)\geq\mathbb P\Big\{\max_iY_i\leq\tau\Big\}.
\] Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) and using right-continuity of distribution functions, \(\mathbb P\{\max X\leq\tau\}\geq\mathbb P\{\max Y\leq\tau\}\), which is the claim.
Expectations. For an integrable random variable \(W\), \[
\mathbb EW=\int_0^\infty\mathbb P\{W>\tau\}\,d\tau-\int_{-\infty}^0\mathbb P\{W\leq\tau\}\,d\tau,
\] and both integrals compare in the right direction.
Separable \(T\). Take finite sets \(T_n\) increasing to a countable dense subset \(T_0\), as in the proof of the Borell–TIS inequality in Lecture 11. The events \(\{\sup_{T_n}X>\tau\}\) increase to \(\{\sup_{T_0}X>\tau\}\), so the tail inequality passes to the limit, and the expectations follow by monotone convergence.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
3 The Sudakov–Fernique inequality
Slepian’s inequality requires equal variances. The Sudakov–Fernique inequality drops that requirement, at the price of comparing only expectations rather than tails. The proof replaces the product of cutoffs by a smooth version of the maximum.

Theorem 2 (Sudakov–Fernique inequality) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) and \((Y_t)_{t\in T}\) be centered Gaussian processes on a set \(T\) whose canonical metric spaces are separable, and suppose that for all \(s,t\in T\), \[
\mathbb E(X_t-X_s)^2\leq\mathbb E(Y_t-Y_s)^2 .
\] Then \(\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\).







NoteProof





By the monotone limit argument it suffices to treat \(T=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and we may take \(X\) and \(Y\) independent. For \(\beta>0\) consider the soft maximum \[
f_\beta(x):=\frac1\beta\log\sum_{i=1}^ne^{\beta x_i},
\qquad
\max_ix_i\leq f_\beta(x)\leq\max_ix_i+\frac{\log n}\beta .
\] Its derivatives are, with \(p_i(x):=e^{\beta x_i}/\sum_ke^{\beta x_k}\), \[
\partial_if_\beta=p_i,
\qquad
\partial_{ij}f_\beta=\beta\big(\delta_{ij}p_i-p_ip_j\big).
\] The \(p_i\) are positive and sum to \(1\), so all derivatives are bounded and Lemma 1 applies. Writing \(D_{ij}:=\Sigma^X_{ij}-\Sigma^Y_{ij}\) and evaluating at \(Z(u)\), \[
\sum_{i,j}D_{ij}\,\partial_{ij}f_\beta
=\beta\Big(\sum_iD_{ii}p_i-\sum_{i,j}D_{ij}p_ip_j\Big).
\] Since \(\sum_jp_j=1\), the first sum equals \(\sum_{i,j}D_{ii}p_ip_j\), and symmetrizing in \(i\) and \(j\) it also equals \(\frac12\sum_{i,j}(D_{ii}+D_{jj})p_ip_j\). Hence \[
\sum_{i,j}D_{ij}\,\partial_{ij}f_\beta
=\frac\beta2\sum_{i,j}p_ip_j\big(D_{ii}+D_{jj}-2D_{ij}\big)
=\frac\beta2\sum_{i,j}p_ip_j\Big(\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2-\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2\Big)\leq0 .
\] By Lemma 1, \(u\mapsto\mathbb Ef_\beta(Z(u))\) is nonincreasing, so \(\mathbb Ef_\beta(X)\leq\mathbb Ef_\beta(Y)\). Therefore \[
\mathbb E\max_iX_i\leq\mathbb Ef_\beta(X)\leq\mathbb Ef_\beta(Y)\leq\mathbb E\max_iY_i+\frac{\log n}\beta ,
\] and \(\beta\to\infty\) finishes the proof.



The inequality has a striking geometric reading. By the Karhunen–Loève theorem of Lecture 10, a centered Gaussian process is the isonormal process restricted to a subset of Hilbert space, and \(\mathbb E\sup X\) is the Gaussian width of that subset. Sudakov–Fernique says that Gaussian width is monotone under contractions: if \(\varphi:x(T)\to y(T)\) is a map between two subsets of Hilbert space that does not increase distances, in the sense that \(\|y(t)-y(s)\|\leq\|x(t)-x(s)\|\), then the width of the image is at most the width of the domain. Nothing about the ambient dimension or the shape of the sets enters.






NoteWhy the variance condition can be dropped





The functional form of Slepian’s lemma needs \(\Sigma^X_{ii}=\Sigma^Y_{ii}\) because the diagonal terms of the interpolation formula carry \(\partial_{ii}f\), whose sign is uncontrolled for a general \(f\) with nonnegative mixed derivatives. The soft maximum is special: its Hessian has the form \(\beta(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\mathsf T})\), which annihilates constants, and this is what allows the diagonal and off-diagonal terms to be regrouped into increments. The price is that \(f_\beta\) approximates only the maximum, not the indicator of \(\{\max\leq\tau\}\), so one obtains expectations and not tails. Tails can be recovered afterwards from Borell–TIS.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
4 Norms of Gaussian random matrices
Lecture 9 proved that an \(m\times n\) matrix with independent isotropic sub-Gaussian rows has \(s_{\max}(A)\leq\sqrt m+CK\sqrt n\) with high probability, by a net argument. For Gaussian entries, comparison gives the constant \(1\).

Theorem 3 (Norm of a Gaussian matrix) Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix with independent \(N(0,1)\) entries. Then \[
\mathbb E\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\sqrt m+\sqrt n .
\]







NoteProof





Write the norm as the supremum of a Gaussian process on \(T=S^{n-1}\times S^{m-1}\): \[
\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{(u,v)\in T}\langle Au,v\rangle=\sup_{(u,v)\in T}X_{uv},
\qquad
X_{uv}:=\langle Au,v\rangle=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}u_jv_i .
\] Each \(X_{uv}\) is \(N(0,1)\), and \(T\) is compact with the process continuous in \((u,v)\), so the supremum convention of Lecture 10 applies.
Increments of \(X\). For \((u,v),(w,z)\in T\), independence of the entries gives \[
\mathbb E(X_{uv}-X_{wz})^2
=\sum_{i,j}\big(u_jv_i-w_jz_i\big)^2
=\|vu^{\mathsf T}-zw^{\mathsf T}\|_F^2
=2-2\langle u,w\rangle\langle v,z\rangle,
\] using \(\|vu^{\mathsf T}\|_F=\|zw^{\mathsf T}\|_F=1\) and \(\langle vu^{\mathsf T},zw^{\mathsf T}\rangle_F=\langle u,w\rangle\langle v,z\rangle\). Now write \(\langle u,w\rangle=1-a\) and \(\langle v,z\rangle=1-b\) with \(a=\|u-w\|_2^2/2\) and \(b=\|v-z\|_2^2/2\), both in \([0,2]\). Then \[
2-2(1-a)(1-b)=2a+2b-2ab=\|u-w\|_2^2+\|v-z\|_2^2-\frac{\|u-w\|_2^2\|v-z\|_2^2}2
\leq\|u-w\|_2^2+\|v-z\|_2^2 .
\]
A simpler process. Let \(g\sim N(0,I_n)\) and \(h\sim N(0,I_m)\) be independent and set \(Y_{uv}:=\langle g,u\rangle+\langle h,v\rangle\). Then \[
\mathbb E(Y_{uv}-Y_{wz})^2=\mathbb E\langle g,u-w\rangle^2+\mathbb E\langle h,v-z\rangle^2
=\|u-w\|_2^2+\|v-z\|_2^2 .
\]
Comparison. The increments of \(X\) are dominated by those of \(Y\), so Theorem 2 gives \[
\mathbb E\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\mathbb E\sup_TX\leq\mathbb E\sup_TY
=\mathbb E\sup_{u\in S^{n-1}}\langle g,u\rangle+\mathbb E\sup_{v\in S^{m-1}}\langle h,v\rangle
=\mathbb E\|g\|_2+\mathbb E\|h\|_2 ,
\] and \(\mathbb E\|g\|_2\leq(\mathbb E\|g\|_2^2)^{1/2}=\sqrt n\), similarly for \(h\).



The proof is the template for every use of comparison. The process of interest is complicated because its index set is a product of spheres and its covariance \(\langle u,w\rangle\langle v,z\rangle\) is a product. The comparison process decouples the two factors into a sum, whose supremum splits and reduces to Gaussian widths of spheres, which Lecture 3 computed. What is lost in the comparison is the product term \(\|u-w\|_2^2\|v-z\|_2^2/2\), and it costs nothing at leading order: in fact \(\mathbb E\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sqrt m+\sqrt n-o(\sqrt n)\) as \(n\to\infty\), though we do not prove this.
Concentration turns the expectation into a tail bound.

Corollary 1 (Tail bound for the norm) In the setting of Theorem 3, for every \(t\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\geq\sqrt m+\sqrt n+t\big\}\leq e^{-t^2/2}.
\]







NoteProof





View \(A\) as a standard Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^{mn}\). The map \(A\mapsto\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb R^{mn}\), which is the Frobenius norm, because \(\big|\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}-\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\big|\leq\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|A-B\|_F\). The Gaussian concentration theorem of Lecture 11 gives \(\mathbb P\{\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\geq\mathbb E\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+t\}\leq e^{-t^2/2}\), and Theorem 3 bounds the mean. Equivalently, this is the Borell–TIS inequality for the process \(X_{uv}\), which has \(\sigma=1\).









NoteThe smallest singular value and Gordon’s inequality





The smallest singular value is a min-max rather than a max, \[
s_{\min}(A)=\min_{u\in S^{n-1}}\max_{v\in S^{m-1}}\langle Au,v\rangle ,
\] and Sudakov–Fernique does not apply to it directly. Gordon’s inequality is the extension of Slepian’s lemma to min-max functionals: for doubly indexed processes \(X_{uv}\) and \(Y_{uv}\) with \(\mathbb E(X_{uv}-X_{uz})^2\leq\mathbb E(Y_{uv}-Y_{uz})^2\) for all \(u,v,z\) and \(\mathbb E(X_{uv}-X_{wz})^2\geq\mathbb E(Y_{uv}-Y_{wz})^2\) for \(u\neq w\), one has \(\mathbb E\min_u\max_vX_{uv}\leq\mathbb E\min_u\max_vY_{uv}\). The proof is the interpolation lemma applied to \(f(x)=\prod_u\big(1-\prod_vh(x_{uv})\big)\), with a sign check for the mixed derivatives that distinguishes pairs sharing the first index from pairs that do not. Applied to the same processes \(X\) and \(Y\) as above, it gives \[
\mathbb Es_{\min}(A)\geq\mathbb E\|h\|_2-\mathbb E\|g\|_2\geq\sqrt m-\sqrt n-\tfrac12 ,
\] using \(\mathbb E\|h\|_2\geq\sqrt m-1/(2\sqrt m)\) from Lecture 3 (the lower bound has the same leading order and the correction is small in practice). Since \(s_{\min}\) is also \(1\)-Lipschitz in the Frobenius norm, \(\mathbb P\{s_{\min}(A)\leq\sqrt m-\sqrt n-\tfrac12-t\}\leq e^{-t^2/2}\). We do not prove Gordon’s inequality here.
Together with Corollary 1, this is the sharp form of the statement that a tall Gaussian matrix is an approximate isometry: with probability \(1-2e^{-t^2/2}\), \[
\sqrt m-\sqrt n-\tfrac12-t\ \leq\ s_{\min}(A)\ \leq\ s_{\max}(A)\ \leq\ \sqrt m+\sqrt n+t .
\] Compare Lecture 9, where the constants in front of \(\sqrt n\) depended on the sub-Gaussian constant of the rows, and Lecture 8, where the distortion did not tend to zero at all.









TipExercise: the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble





Let \(A\) be a symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix whose entries above the diagonal are independent \(N(0,1)\) and whose diagonal entries are independent \(N(0,2)\). Show that \(\mathbb E\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq2\sqrt n\) and \(\mathbb P\{\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\geq2\sqrt n+t\}\leq e^{-t^2/4}\).
Hint. Check that \(\mathbb E\langle Au,u\rangle\langle Aw,w\rangle=2\langle u,w\rangle^2\) for unit \(u,w\). For \(\lambda_{\max}(A)=\sup_u\langle Au,u\rangle\) compare with \(Y_u=2\langle g,u\rangle\) using \(1-c^2\leq2(1-c)\) for \(|c|\leq1\). For \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{(u,\varepsilon)}\varepsilon\langle Au,u\rangle\) over \(S^{n-1}\times\{\pm1\}\) compare with \(Y_{u,\varepsilon}=2\varepsilon\langle g,u\rangle\), checking the increments for pairs with opposite signs separately. The tail bound uses that \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) is \(\sqrt2\)-Lipschitz in the Gaussian coordinates that parametrize \(A\).

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
5 Sudakov’s minoration
Lecture 3 stated that Gaussian width controls covering numbers at every scale and left the proof as a roadmap, because it needed a comparison theorem. Here is the proof, for a general Gaussian process.

Theorem 4 (Sudakov’s minoration inequality) There is an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that for every centered Gaussian process \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) with separable canonical metric \(d\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\geq c\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N(T,d,\varepsilon)} .
\] For the Gaussian width process \(X_t=\langle g,t\rangle\) on \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) this reads \(w(T)\geq c\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N(T,\|\cdot\|_2,\varepsilon)}\).







NoteProof





We need a lower bound on the expected maximum of independent Gaussians: for \(N\geq2\) and \(g\sim N(0,I_N)\), \[
\mathbb E\max_{i\leq N}g_i\geq c_0\sqrt{\log N} .
\] Indeed, \(\max_i|g_i|\leq\max_ig_i+\max_i(-g_i)\), and the two terms on the right have the same law, so \(\mathbb E\max_ig_i\geq\frac12\mathbb E\|g\|_\infty\), and Exercise Sheet 2 showed \(\mathbb E\|g\|_\infty\geq\sqrt{2\log N}-o(1)\) as \(N\to\infty\). For each fixed \(N\geq2\) the left side is positive, so a single constant \(c_0\) works for all \(N\geq2\).
Now let \(N:=N(T,d,\varepsilon)\), which we may assume finite and at least \(2\), the statement being trivial otherwise (if \(N=\infty\), run the argument on finite subsets). By the covering–packing comparison of Lecture 1, \(T\) contains an \(\varepsilon\)-separated set \(t_1,\ldots,t_N\). Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) be independent \(N(0,\varepsilon^2/2)\). For \(i\neq j\), \[
\mathbb E(X_{t_i}-X_{t_j})^2=d(t_i,t_j)^2\geq\varepsilon^2=\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2 .
\] So \(Y\) has the smaller increments, and Theorem 2 applied to the processes \((Y_i)\) and \((X_{t_i})\) on the finite set \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) gives \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\geq\mathbb E\max_{i\leq N}X_{t_i}\geq\mathbb E\max_{i\leq N}Y_i
=\frac\varepsilon{\sqrt2}\,\mathbb E\max_{i\leq N}g_i\geq\frac{c_0}{\sqrt2}\,\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N} .
\]



Sudakov’s inequality is a statement about a single scale: it says nothing about how the covering numbers at different scales combine. Its converse direction, an upper bound on \(\mathbb E\sup X\) from the covering numbers, requires all scales at once and is Dudley’s inequality, the subject of the chaining lectures. The two together bracket the expected supremum between the entropy at the worst single scale and the integral of the entropy over all scales.






NoteSudakov as a geometric measurement





For the Gaussian width process the inequality reads \[
\log N(T,\varepsilon)\leq\frac{C\,w(T)^2}{\varepsilon^2}
\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0 .
\] This is a purely geometric statement about subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), proved by probabilistic means. For the \(\ell^p\) balls with \(1\leq p\leq2\), Lecture 3 and its exercises give \(w(B_p^d)\asymp d^{1-1/p}\) up to logarithmic factors at \(p=1\), so \[
\log N(B_p^d,\varepsilon)\lesssim\frac{d^{2-2/p}}{\varepsilon^2},
\] which for \(p<2\) is subexponential in \(d\) at fixed \(\varepsilon\), far below the volumetric bound \(d\log(C/\varepsilon)\). At \(p=1\) this recovers the Maurey bound of Lecture 2 up to logarithms, by a completely different argument. For \(p>2\) the volumetric bound is the better one, and Sudakov is not sharp.

title: Lecture 12: Gaussian Comparison and Gaussian Matrices
text:
6 Where we go next
Comparison inequalities compute expected suprema by trading a complicated process for a simpler one with larger increments. The next lecture returns to Gaussian width with these tools in hand: Sudakov’s minoration as a geometric measurement, the width of sparse vectors and of \(\ell^p\) balls, and Gaussian width as the quantity that governs the diameter of a random projection of a set and the intersection of randomly rotated cones. After that, the semidefinite relaxation lectures use the Gaussian tools of Lectures 10 and 11 in a different direction, to round the solution of a convex program to a point of the discrete cube.

title: Lecture 10: Gaussian Processes
text: Several objects from earlier lectures are random functions of a parameter. The Gaussian width of Lecture 3 is the expected supremum of \(t\mapsto\langle g,t\rangle\) over a set \(T\). The singular values of a Gaussian matrix are the extreme values of \((u,v)\mapsto\langle Au,v\rangle\) over pairs of unit vectors. In each case the random function is jointly Gaussian, and Lecture 9 ended by claiming that the sharpest results about such functions come not from discretizing the parameter set but from comparing one Gaussian function to another. This lecture sets up the language for that: Gaussian processes, the metric they induce on their index set, and the two tools, the isonormal process and Stein’s lemma, on which the next two lectures rest.

title: Lecture 10: Gaussian Processes
text:
1 The multivariate normal

Definition 1 (Gaussian random vector) A random vector \(X\) in \(\mathbb R^d\) is Gaussian, written \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\), if there are \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a positive semidefinite \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) such that \[
\mathbb Ee^{i\langle\xi,X\rangle}=\exp\Big(i\langle\xi,\mu\rangle-\frac12\langle\xi,\Sigma\xi\rangle\Big)
\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in\mathbb R^d .
\] Then \(\mu=\mathbb EX\) and \(\Sigma=\mathbb E(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\).

The definition through the characteristic function makes the basic manipulations immediate, because the characteristic function determines the law and behaves well under linear maps.

Proposition 1 (Linear images and the square-root representation)  

If \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^k\), then \(AX+b\sim N(A\mu+b,\ A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T})\).
If \(Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)\) has i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\) coordinates, then \(Z\sim N(0,I_d)\), and \(\mu+AZ\sim N(\mu,AA^{\mathsf T})\) for every \(A\).
Conversely, if \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\), then \(X\) has the same law as \(\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z\), where \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) is the positive semidefinite square root of \(\Sigma\). In particular \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) exists for every \(\mu\) and every positive semidefinite \(\Sigma\).
If \(\Sigma\) is invertible, \(X\) has density \((2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\big(-\frac12\langle x-\mu,\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\rangle\big)\).








NoteProof





For (1), \[
\mathbb Ee^{i\langle\xi,AX+b\rangle}
=e^{i\langle\xi,b\rangle}\,\mathbb Ee^{i\langle A^{\mathsf T}\xi,X\rangle}
=\exp\Big(i\langle\xi,A\mu+b\rangle-\frac12\langle A^{\mathsf T}\xi,\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}\xi\rangle\Big),
\] and \(\langle A^{\mathsf T}\xi,\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}\xi\rangle=\langle\xi,A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}\xi\rangle\). For (2), independence factors the characteristic function of \(Z\) into \(\prod_je^{-\xi_j^2/2}=e^{-\|\xi\|_2^2/2}\), and then (1) applies. For (3), by (2) the vector \(\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), and two random vectors with the same characteristic function have the same law. For (4), change variables in the density of \(Z\) using the map \(z\mapsto\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}z\), whose Jacobian is \((\det\Sigma)^{1/2}\).



Two consequences are used constantly.
Rotation invariance. If \(U\) is orthogonal and \(Z\sim N(0,I_d)\), then \(UZ\sim N(0,UU^{\mathsf T})=N(0,I_d)\). The standard Gaussian vector has no preferred direction.
Independence is a matter of covariance. If \(X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)\) and \(\Sigma\) is block diagonal with respect to a splitting of the coordinates, then the characteristic function factors over the blocks, so the corresponding sub-vectors of \(X\) are independent. For jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelated means independent. This is false without joint Gaussianity, and it is the reason the joint law matters in the definition of a Gaussian process below.
For a standard Gaussian vector \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and fixed \(u,v\in\mathbb R^d\), part (1) gives \[
\langle g,u\rangle\sim N(0,\|u\|_2^2),
\qquad
\mathbb E\langle g,u\rangle\langle g,v\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle .
\] So the linear forms of a standard Gaussian vector reproduce the Euclidean geometry of \(\mathbb R^d\) inside a space of random variables. This observation is the seed of the whole lecture.

title: Lecture 10: Gaussian Processes
section: 2 Gaussian processes and the canonical metric
text:
2 Gaussian processes and the canonical metric
