\] and since \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), \[
\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\Big\|\frac1mA^{\mathsf T}A-I_n\Big\|_{\mathrm{op}} .
\] The expectation bound is now Corollary 1. For the tail bound, apply Theorem 1 with \(t=\sqrt u\). Then \(\delta=C(\sqrt{n/m}+\sqrt{u/m})\leq2C\sqrt{(n+u)/m}\), and \(K\max\{\delta,\delta^2\}\leq K(\delta+\delta^2)\) gives the claim.









NoteSample complexity





Fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). The theorem gives relative error \(\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\varepsilon\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) as soon as \[
m\geq\frac{C'K^2n}{\varepsilon^2}.
\] So the sample covariance is an accurate estimate of the covariance once the number of samples is a constant multiple of the dimension, and the constant scales like \(\varepsilon^{-2}\), the usual price of a relative error \(\varepsilon\) in a variance estimate. This matches the necessary condition \(m\geq n\) up to the constant.









NoteUncentered data





If \(X\) has an unknown mean \(\mu\), the theorem applies verbatim to the second moment matrix \(\mathbb EXX^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma+\mu\mu^{\mathsf T}\), provided the sub-Gaussian hypothesis is placed on \(\langle X-\mu,x\rangle\) and the mean is not too large relative to \(\Sigma\). Estimating \(\Sigma\) itself requires subtracting the sample mean, which adds an error of order \(\|\bar X_m-\mu\|_2^2\), and this is of smaller order than the main term. We omit the bookkeeping.

title: Lecture 9: Covariance Estimation
text:
6 What the rate cannot see
The bound \(\sqrt{n/m}\) depends on the ambient dimension and on nothing else about \(\Sigma\). Two remarks put this in perspective.
The rate is sharp for isotropic data. If \(X\sim N(0,I_n)\) then \(\Sigma_m=\frac1mA^{\mathsf T}A\) for a Gaussian matrix \(A\), and its extreme eigenvalues are \(s_{\min}(A)^2/m\) and \(s_{\max}(A)^2/m\). Lecture 12 shows that for Gaussian matrices \[
\mathbb Es_{\max}(A)\leq\sqrt m+\sqrt n,
\qquad
\mathbb Es_{\min}(A)\geq\sqrt m-\sqrt n,
\] and both bounds are attained to leading order. The eigenvalues of \(\Sigma_m\) therefore spread over an interval of half-width about \(2\sqrt{n/m}\) around \(1\), and \(\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\approx2\sqrt{n/m}\). In fact the whole empirical spectrum of \(\Sigma_m\) has a deterministic limiting shape, the Marchenko–Pastur law (Marchenko and Pastur 1967), supported on exactly this interval.

Marchenko, Vladimir A., and Leonid A. Pastur. 1967. “Distribution of Eigenvalues for Some Sets of Random Matrices.” Mathematics of the USSR-Sbornik 1 (4): 457–83.

Koltchinskii, Vladimir, and Karim Lounici. 2017. “Concentration Inequalities and Moment Bounds for Sample Covariance Operators.” Bernoulli 23 (1): 110–33. https://doi.org/10.3150/15-BEJ730.
But the dimension is the wrong parameter for structured data. Suppose the data are nearly low-dimensional: \(\Sigma\) has a few large eigenvalues and many small ones. The theorem still charges for all \(n\) directions, even though the small directions contribute almost nothing to \(\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). The correct parameter is the effective rank \[
r(\Sigma):=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\in[1,n],
\] which equals \(n\) for isotropic data and stays bounded when the spectrum decays fast. For Gaussian data one has \[
\mathbb E\|\Sigma_m-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C\Big(\sqrt{\frac{r(\Sigma)}m}+\frac{r(\Sigma)}m\Big)\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}},
\] a theorem of Koltchinskii and Lounici (Koltchinskii and Lounici 2017). The net argument of this lecture cannot prove it. The proof of Theorem 1 pays \(n\log12\) for the net regardless of the geometry of \(\Sigma\), and no choice of net on the ellipsoid \(\Sigma^{1/2}S^{n-1}\) repairs this. What is needed is a way to control \(\sup_x|\frac1m\|Ax\|_2^2-\|x\|_2^2|\) over the ellipsoid that sees its shape and not only its dimension. That is what the theory of Gaussian processes provides, and Lecture 20 proves the effective-rank theorem with it.

title: Lecture 9: Covariance Estimation
text:
7 Where we go next
Two loose ends of this lecture point in the same direction. The constant in \(\sqrt m\pm CK\sqrt n\) should be \(1\) for Gaussian matrices, and the dimension \(n\) in the covariance bound should be the effective rank. Both statements are about the random function \(x\mapsto\|Ax\|_2\) on a set of vectors, and both are proved by comparing it to simpler Gaussian processes rather than by discretizing the set. The next lectures develop Gaussian processes from the beginning: their construction, their concentration, and the comparison inequalities that make them computable.

title: Lecture 11: Gaussian Concentration
text: Lecture 10 ended with two questions about the supremum of a Gaussian process: how large is it, and how concentrated is it around its mean? This lecture answers the second, and the answer is remarkably clean. The supremum fluctuates on the scale of the largest standard deviation of a single \(X_t\), whatever the index set. The mechanism is a concentration inequality for Lipschitz functions of a Gaussian vector, proved with Stein’s lemma, and the passage from Lipschitz functions to suprema is the observation that a maximum of linear functions is Lipschitz.

title: Lecture 11: Gaussian Concentration
text:
1 The Gaussian concentration inequality
Throughout, \(\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\) denotes the Lipschitz constant of a function \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) with respect to the Euclidean norm. For such \(h\), \(\nabla h\) exists almost everywhere and \(\|\nabla h\|_2\leq\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\) wherever it exists.

Theorem 1 (Gaussian concentration) Let \(X\sim N(0,I_d)\) and let \(h:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz. Then for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), \[
\mathbb Ee^{\lambda(h(X)-\mathbb Eh(X))}\leq\exp\Big(\frac{\lambda^2\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}^2}2\Big),
\] and consequently, for every \(t\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{|h(X)-\mathbb Eh(X)|\geq t\big\}\leq2\exp\Big(-\frac{t^2}{2\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}^2}\Big).
\]

In the language of Lecture 4, \(h(X)-\mathbb Eh(X)\) is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}^2\). The dimension \(d\) does not appear. A \(1\)-Lipschitz function of a standard Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^{10^6}\) fluctuates no more than a \(1\)-Lipschitz function of a single standard Gaussian, which is to say no more than \(N(0,1)\) itself. The linear function \(h(x)=x_1\) shows that the constant in the exponent cannot be improved.
The proof rests on an interpolation identity for covariances. For \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) and independent \(X,Y\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), set \[
X_\alpha:=\alpha X+\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,Y .
\] Then \(X_\alpha\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) for every \(\alpha\), since \(\alpha^2+(1-\alpha^2)=1\), while \(X_1=X\) and \(X_0=Y\) is independent of \(X\). The path \(\alpha\mapsto X_\alpha\) moves from a copy of \(X\) to an independent copy without leaving the distribution \(N(0,\Sigma)\).

Lemma 1 (Covariance interpolation) Let \(X,Y\) be independent \(N(0,\Sigma)\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\), let \(f\) be Lipschitz, and let \(g\) be \(C^1\) and Lipschitz. Then \[
\operatorname{Cov}\big(f(X),g(X)\big)
=\int_0^1\mathbb E\big\langle\Sigma\nabla f(X),\nabla g(X_\alpha)\big\rangle\,d\alpha .
\]







NoteProof





Since \(X_1=X\) and \(X_0=Y\) is independent of \(X\), \[
\operatorname{Cov}\big(f(X),g(X)\big)
=\mathbb Ef(X)g(X_1)-\mathbb Ef(X)g(X_0)
=\mathbb E\Big[f(X)\int_0^1\frac d{d\alpha}g(X_\alpha)\,d\alpha\Big].
\] For \(0<\alpha<1\), the chain rule gives \[
\frac d{d\alpha}g(X_\alpha)
=\Big\langle\nabla g(X_\alpha),\,X-\frac\alpha{\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}}Y\Big\rangle
=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}}\big\langle\nabla g(X_\alpha),W_\alpha\big\rangle,
\qquad
W_\alpha:=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,X-\alpha Y .
\] The pair \((X_\alpha,W_\alpha)\) is a rotation of \((X,Y)\) by an angle: both are \(N(0,\Sigma)\), and \[
\mathbb EX_\alpha W_\alpha^{\mathsf T}
=\alpha\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,\Sigma-\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,\alpha\,\Sigma=0,
\] so by the independence remark of Lecture 10 they are independent. Inverting the rotation, \(X=\alpha X_\alpha+\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,W_\alpha\).
Fix \(\alpha\) and condition on \(X_\alpha\). The function \(w\mapsto f(\alpha X_\alpha+\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,w)\) is Lipschitz with gradient \(\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,\nabla f(X)\), and \(W_\alpha\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) is independent of \(X_\alpha\). The multivariate Stein lemma of Lecture 10, applied coordinate by coordinate to \(W_\alpha\), gives \[
\mathbb E\big[f(X)\langle\nabla g(X_\alpha),W_\alpha\rangle\,\big|\,X_\alpha\big]
=\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\,\mathbb E\big[\langle\nabla g(X_\alpha),\Sigma\nabla f(X)\rangle\,\big|\,X_\alpha\big].
\] Taking expectations, dividing by \(\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\), and integrating in \(\alpha\) gives the identity. The interchange of \(\int_0^1d\alpha\) and \(\mathbb E\) is justified by Fubini, since the integrand is bounded by \(|f(X)|\,\|g\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\,\|W_\alpha\|_2/\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}\), whose expectation is integrable in \(\alpha\) on \((0,1)\).









NoteProof of the concentration inequality





Replacing \(h\) by \(h-\mathbb Eh(X)\) we may assume \(\mathbb Eh(X)=0\). Write \(L=\|h\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\). Assume first that \(h\) is \(C^1\) and bounded, so that \(g:=e^{\lambda h}\) is \(C^1\) and Lipschitz for every \(\lambda\).
Let \(M(\lambda):=\mathbb Ee^{\lambda h(X)}\), so that \(M(0)=1\) and \(M'(\lambda)=\mathbb Eh(X)e^{\lambda h(X)}\). Since \(\mathbb Eh(X)=0\), this is a covariance, and Lemma 1 with \(\Sigma=I_d\), \(f=h\) and \(g=e^{\lambda h}\) gives \[
M'(\lambda)=\operatorname{Cov}\big(h(X),e^{\lambda h(X)}\big)
=\lambda\int_0^1\mathbb E\Big[\big\langle\nabla h(X),\nabla h(X_\alpha)\big\rangle e^{\lambda h(X_\alpha)}\Big]d\alpha .
\] For \(\lambda\geq0\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\langle\nabla h(X),\nabla h(X_\alpha)\rangle\leq L^2\) pointwise, and \(X_\alpha\sim N(0,I_d)\) for every \(\alpha\), so \[
M'(\lambda)\leq\lambda L^2\int_0^1\mathbb Ee^{\lambda h(X_\alpha)}\,d\alpha=\lambda L^2M(\lambda).
\] Hence \((\log M)'(\lambda)\leq\lambda L^2\), and integrating from \(0\), \[
M(\lambda)\leq\exp\Big(\frac{\lambda^2L^2}2\Big)
\qquad(\lambda\geq0).
\] Applying this to \(-h\) handles \(\lambda<0\). So \(h(X)\) is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(L^2\), and the tail bound is the sub-Gaussian tail bound of Lecture 4.
For a general Lipschitz \(h\), the extra assumptions are removed by approximation; see the aside below.









NoteRemoving the smoothness and boundedness assumptions





Let \(h\) be Lipschitz with constant \(L\) and mean zero under \(N(0,I_d)\). First truncate: \(h_M:=\max\{\min\{h,M\},-M\}\) is bounded and still \(L\)-Lipschitz. Then smooth: for \(\varepsilon>0\) let \(h_{M,\varepsilon}:=h_M*\varphi_\varepsilon\) be the convolution with the density of \(N(0,\varepsilon^2I_d)\). Convolution with a probability density preserves the Lipschitz constant and the bound \(M\), and makes the function \(C^\infty\). So the moment generating function bound holds for \(h_{M,\varepsilon}-\mathbb Eh_{M,\varepsilon}(X)\) with the same \(L\).
As \(\varepsilon\to0\), \(h_{M,\varepsilon}\to h_M\) uniformly, because \(|h_{M,\varepsilon}(x)-h_M(x)|\leq L\,\mathbb E\|\varepsilon Z\|_2\leq L\varepsilon\sqrt d\). As \(M\to\infty\), \(h_M\to h\) pointwise with \(|h_M|\leq|h|\), and \(h(X)\) has Gaussian tails since \(|h(x)|\leq|h(0)|+L\|x\|_2\). Dominated convergence passes the bound \(\mathbb Ee^{\lambda(h_{M,\varepsilon}(X)-\mathbb Eh_{M,\varepsilon}(X))}\leq e^{\lambda^2L^2/2}\) to the limit in each step.



Two immediate applications recover, and sharpen, results seen earlier.
The norm. The function \(x\mapsto\|x\|_2\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, so \[
\mathbb P\big\{\big|\|X\|_2-\mathbb E\|X\|_2\big|\geq t\big\}\leq2e^{-t^2/2}
\qquad(t\geq0).
\] Lecture 3 and Exercise Sheet 3 obtained this for Gaussian vectors by a Bernstein argument on \(\|X\|_2^2\). Here it is a one-line consequence of a general principle, with an explicit constant.
The Gaussian width process. Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be bounded with \(R:=\sup_{t\in T}\|t\|_2\), and let \(h_T(x)=\sup_{t\in T}\langle x,t\rangle\) be its support function. For every \(t\in T\), \(\langle x,t\rangle\leq\langle y,t\rangle+R\|x-y\|_2\leq h_T(y)+R\|x-y\|_2\), so \(h_T\) is \(R\)-Lipschitz. Therefore \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\Big|\sup_{t\in T}\langle g,t\rangle-w(T)\Big|\geq u\Big\}\leq2\exp\Big(-\frac{u^2}{2R^2}\Big).
\] The mean of the supremum is the Gaussian width, a quantity that reflects the whole geometry of \(T\). The fluctuations depend on \(T\) only through its radius. These are different pieces of information, and the second is far cruder than the first: for \(T=B_2^d\) the mean is about \(\sqrt d\) while the fluctuations are of order \(1\).

title: Lecture 11: Gaussian Concentration
text:
2 Concentration on the sphere
The uniform distribution on the sphere inherits concentration from the Gaussian, because a normalized Gaussian vector is uniform on the sphere and the normalization is nearly constant.

Theorem 2 (Concentration on the sphere) There are absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that the following holds. Let \(\omega\) be uniform on \(S^{d-1}\) and let \(f:S^{d-1}\to\mathbb R\) be Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean distance, with constant \(L\). Then for every \(t\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{|f(\omega)-\mathbb Ef(\omega)|\geq t\big\}\leq C\exp\Big(-\frac{c\,dt^2}{L^2}\Big).
\]

The point is the factor \(d\) in the exponent. A \(1\)-Lipschitz function on the sphere of radius \(1\) fluctuates by about \(1/\sqrt d\), which is the scale on which the sphere looks flat. This is the same phenomenon as the volume concentration of Lecture 1: the sphere of radius \(\sqrt d\), on which a \(1\)-Lipschitz function fluctuates by \(O(1)\), is the sphere on which the standard Gaussian vector lives.






NoteProof





By homogeneity take \(L=1\), and by subtracting a constant assume \(|f|\leq2\), which is possible because \(f\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz on a set of diameter \(2\). Let \(Z\sim N(0,I_d)\); by rotation invariance, \(\omega\) has the law of \(Z/\|Z\|_2\), and we work with this representation.
Step 1: a Lipschitz extension. Let \(\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]\) be the piecewise linear function equal to \(1\) on \([\sqrt d/2,2\sqrt d]\), equal to \(0\) outside \([\sqrt d/4,3\sqrt d]\), and linear in between; its Lipschitz constant is \(4/\sqrt d\). Define \[
F(z):=\varphi(\|z\|_2)\,f\Big(\frac z{\|z\|_2}\Big),
\qquad F(0):=0 .
\] We claim \(F\) is \((16/\sqrt d)\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(z_1,z_2\neq0\), \[
|F(z_1)-F(z_2)|
\leq\big|\varphi(\|z_1\|_2)-\varphi(\|z_2\|_2)\big|\cdot2
+\varphi(\|z_2\|_2)\,\Big\|\frac{z_1}{\|z_1\|_2}-\frac{z_2}{\|z_2\|_2}\Big\|_2 .
\] The first term is at most \((8/\sqrt d)\|z_1-z_2\|_2\). For the second, the elementary inequality \(\|a/\|a\|_2-b/\|b\|_2\|_2\leq2\|a-b\|_2/\|b\|_2\) and the fact that \(\varphi(\|z_2\|_2)\neq0\) forces \(\|z_2\|_2\geq\sqrt d/4\) bound it by \((8/\sqrt d)\|z_1-z_2\|_2\). The cases involving \(z=0\) are similar.
Step 2: concentration of \(F(Z)\). By Theorem 1, \[
\mathbb P\big\{|F(Z)-\mathbb EF(Z)|\geq s\big\}\leq2\exp\Big(-\frac{ds^2}{512}\Big).
\]
Step 3: comparing \(F(Z)\) with \(f(\omega)\). Let \(E=\{\sqrt d/2\leq\|Z\|_2\leq2\sqrt d\}\). On \(E\), \(F(Z)=f(\omega)\). By the Bernstein bound on \(\|Z\|_2^2\) from Lecture 6, \(\mathbb P\{E^c\}\leq2e^{-c_0d}\) for an absolute \(c_0>0\). Since \(|F(Z)-f(\omega)|=(1-\varphi(\|Z\|_2))|f(\omega)|\leq2\) always, \[
|\mathbb EF(Z)-\mathbb Ef(\omega)|\leq2\,\mathbb P\{E^c\}\leq4e^{-c_0d}.
\] Hence for \(t\geq8e^{-c_0d}\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{|f(\omega)-\mathbb Ef(\omega)|\geq t\big\}
\leq\mathbb P\{E^c\}+\mathbb P\big\{|F(Z)-\mathbb EF(Z)|\geq t/2\big\}
\leq2e^{-c_0d}+2e^{-dt^2/2048}.
\] Since \(|f(\omega)-\mathbb Ef(\omega)|\leq2\), only \(t\leq2\) matters, and for such \(t\) we have \(e^{-c_0d}\leq e^{-c_0dt^2/4}\). This gives the claim for \(t\geq8e^{-c_0d}\) with \(c=\min\{c_0/4,1/2048\}\) and \(C=4\). For smaller \(t\), the right-hand side of the claim exceeds \(1\) once \(C\) is increased to an absolute constant, because \(dt^2\leq64de^{-2c_0d}\) is bounded uniformly in \(d\).



The constants here are far from optimal. The sharp statement, due to Lévy, is that spherical caps are the extremal sets, which gives the exponent \(-(d-2)t^2/(2L^2)\). The proof above trades the constant for the convenience of deducing the sphere from the Gaussian, which is the pattern we follow throughout.

title: Lecture 11: Gaussian Concentration
text:
3 The Borell–TIS inequality
The Gaussian width process was concentrated because its supremum is a Lipschitz function of \(g\). The same is true of every Gaussian process, via the Karhunen–Loève representation of Lecture 10, and the Lipschitz constant is the largest standard deviation.

Theorem 3 (Borell–TIS inequality) Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) be a centered Gaussian process whose canonical metric space \((T,d)\) is separable. Suppose \[
\sigma^2:=\sup_{t\in T}\mathbb EX_t^2<\infty
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t<\infty .
\] Then for every \(x\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{t\in T}X_t-\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\geq x\Big\}\leq e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)},
\qquad
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{t\in T}X_t-\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\leq-x\Big\}\leq e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}.
\]







NoteProof





Finite index sets. Let \(T'=\{t_1,\ldots,t_n\}\subseteq T\) be finite and let \(\Sigma\) be the covariance matrix of \((X_{t_i})_{i\leq n}\). By the square-root representation of Lecture 10, this vector has the law of \(\Sigma^{1/2}Z\) with \(Z\sim N(0,I_n)\). Define \[
\varphi(z):=\max_{i\leq n}\big(\Sigma^{1/2}z\big)_i ,
\] so that \(\sup_{t\in T'}X_t\) has the law of \(\varphi(Z)\). Each coordinate function \(z\mapsto(\Sigma^{1/2}z)_i=\langle(\Sigma^{1/2})_{i\cdot},z\rangle\) is Lipschitz with constant \(\|(\Sigma^{1/2})_{i\cdot}\|_2=\sqrt{(\Sigma)_{ii}}=\sqrt{\mathbb EX_{t_i}^2}\leq\sigma\), and a maximum of \(\sigma\)-Lipschitz functions is \(\sigma\)-Lipschitz. By Theorem 1, both one-sided bounds hold for \(T'\), each with the single-tail constant \(1\) in front (the proof of the concentration theorem bounds each tail separately by \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\)).
Passage to the limit. Let \(T_0\) be a countable dense subset of \((T,d)\) and let \(T_1\subseteq T_2\subseteq\cdots\) be finite sets increasing to \(T_0\). By the convention of Lecture 10, \(\sup_TX=\sup_{T_0}X\), and \(S_n:=\sup_{T_n}X\) increases to \(S:=\sup_{T_0}X\) almost surely. By monotone convergence, \(\mathbb ES_n\uparrow\mathbb ES\), which is finite by hypothesis. Fix \(x\geq0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), and let \(n\) be large enough that \(\mathbb ES_n\geq\mathbb ES-\varepsilon\). Then \[
\{S_n-\mathbb ES>x\}\subseteq\{S_n-\mathbb ES_n\geq x-\varepsilon\},
\] so \(\mathbb P\{S_n-\mathbb ES>x\}\leq e^{-(x-\varepsilon)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) for all large \(n\). The events \(\{S_n-\mathbb ES>x\}\) increase to \(\{S-\mathbb ES>x\}\), hence \(\mathbb P\{S-\mathbb ES>x\}\leq e^{-(x-\varepsilon)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). Let \(\varepsilon\to0\), then replace \(x\) by \(x-\varepsilon'\) and let \(\varepsilon'\to0\) to pass from \(>x\) to \(\geq x\). The lower tail is the same argument with the inequalities reversed, using \(S_n\leq S\) and \(\mathbb ES_n\leq\mathbb ES\) directly.



The theorem is the answer to the concentration question. Whatever the index set, the supremum of a Gaussian process is sub-Gaussian around its mean with variance proxy \(\sigma^2\), the largest variance of a single \(X_t\). Some remarks.
The mean dominates the fluctuations. Applying the theorem to the process \((\varepsilon X_t)_{(t,\varepsilon)\in T\times\{\pm1\}}\), whose supremum is \(\sup_t|X_t|\), gives the same bounds for \(\sup_t|X_t|\). But \(\mathbb E\sup_t|X_t|\geq\sup_t\mathbb E|X_t|=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma\), so the mean of \(\sup|X_t|\) is always at least a constant multiple of the scale \(\sigma\) on which it fluctuates. The supremum of a Gaussian process is therefore never much more spread out than it is large. This is why the remaining problem, taken up in Lecture 12, is the mean alone.
Finiteness of the mean is a genuine hypothesis. For i.i.d. standard Gaussians indexed by \(\mathbb N\) we have \(\sigma=1\) but \(\sup_tX_t=+\infty\), and the theorem says nothing. Conversely, when \(\mathbb E\sup X<\infty\), the theorem shows that \(\sup X\) has Gaussian tails, so all its moments are finite.
No independence, no structure. The proof used nothing about \(T\). Every concentration statement earlier in the course, from Hoeffding to Bernstein, required independent summands. Here the \(X_t\) may be arbitrarily correlated.






NoteExample: the maximum of \(d\) independent Gaussians





Let \(G\sim N(0,I_d)\) and consider \(\|G\|_\infty=\max_i|G_i|\), a Gaussian supremum with \(\sigma=1\) over the index set \(\{\pm e_1,\ldots,\pm e_d\}\). Lecture 3 gives \(\mathbb E\|G\|_\infty\leq\sqrt{2\log(2d)}\), and it is also at least \(\sqrt{2\log d}-o(1)\).
Upper tail by a union bound. Using the Gaussian tail \(\mathbb P\{|Z|\geq s\}\leq e^{-s^2/2}\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{\|G\|_\infty\geq\sqrt{2\log d}+t\big\}
\leq d\,e^{-(\sqrt{2\log d}+t)^2/2}
=e^{-t\sqrt{2\log d}-t^2/2}.
\]
Both tails by Borell–TIS. With \(m=\mathbb E\|G\|_\infty\), \[
\mathbb P\big\{|\|G\|_\infty-m|\geq t\big\}\leq2e^{-t^2/2}.
\]
The union bound gives the better upper tail, which is not surprising: it used the independence of the coordinates and the exact Gaussian tail, while Borell–TIS used only \(\sigma=1\). What Borell–TIS adds is the lower tail, \(\mathbb P\{\|G\|_\infty\leq m-t\}\leq e^{-t^2/2}\), which no union bound can produce, and which it produces with no independence at all.
Both bounds miss the truth. In fact \(\|G\|_\infty-\sqrt{2\log d}\to0\) in probability, and the fluctuations of \(\|G\|_\infty\) are of order \(1/\sqrt{\log d}\), not order \(1\). Borell–TIS is sharp for some processes (a single \(X_t\), for instance) but it is a worst-case statement over all index sets with a given \(\sigma\), and it cannot see the finer structure of a particular one.

title: Lecture 11: Gaussian Concentration
text:
4 Where we go next
Concentration reduces the study of \(\sup_tX_t\) to the study of its mean. The next lecture develops the main tool for the mean, Gaussian comparison. Slepian’s inequality and the Sudakov–Fernique inequality say that if the canonical metric of one process is dominated by that of another, then so is the expected supremum. The proof is again Stein’s lemma along an interpolation between two Gaussian vectors, now with two different covariances at the endpoints. The first application is the norm of a Gaussian random matrix, where comparison gives the sharp bound \(\sqrt m+\sqrt n\) and Borell–TIS turns it into a tail bound.

title: Lecture 13: Gaussian Width Revisited
text:
Lecture 3 introduced the Gaussian width \(w(T)=\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}\langle g,t\rangle\) as a measure of the size of a set, computed it for a few standard sets, and left two things unfinished: the width of the set of sparse vectors, and the proof of Sudakov’s minoration. Lecture 12 supplied the proof. This lecture uses the tools of Lectures 10 through 12 to finish the sparse example and then to show what Gaussian width is for. It governs the size of a random projection of a set, with a phase transition at a dimension-like quantity built from the width, and it governs whether two randomly rotated cones intersect. In both problems the ambient dimension is the wrong parameter and the width is the right one.
Throughout, \(g\sim N(0,I_n)\) and \(w(T)=\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}\langle g,t\rangle\) for bounded \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Recall from Lecture 3 that \(w(T)=w(\operatorname{conv}T)\) and \(w(T-T)=2w(T)\), and from Lecture 12 that Sudakov’s minoration reads \[
\log N(T,\varepsilon)\leq\frac{C\,w(T)^2}{\varepsilon^2}
\qquad(\varepsilon>0).
\]

title: Lecture 13: Gaussian Width Revisited
text:
1 Sparse vectors
Let \(1\leq s\leq n\) and let \[
U_s:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\leq1,\ |\operatorname{supp}x|\leq s\}
\] be the set of \(s\)-sparse vectors in the unit ball. Lecture 3 claimed \(w(U_s)\asymp\sqrt{s\log(en/s)}\) and observed that \(U_s\) is neither finite nor convex, so that neither tool available then applied. Both bounds are now within reach.

Proposition 1 (Width of the sparse vectors) There are absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that, for \(1\leq s\leq n/2\) with \(n/s\) larger than an absolute constant, \[
c\sqrt{s\log(en/s)}\leq w(U_s)\leq C\sqrt{s\log(en/s)} .
\]







NoteProof





Upper bound. This is Problem 4 of Exercise Sheet 3. The supremum over \(U_s\) is \(\max_{|S|=s}\|g_S\|_2\), a maximum over \(\binom ns\) chi variables, and the exponential-moment argument of Lecture 3 for finite sets, applied to the squares, gives \(\mathbb E\max_S\|g_S\|_2^2\leq Cs\log(en/s)\). Jensen’s inequality finishes.
Lower bound. The packing lemma of Lecture 2 provides a family \(X\) of \(s\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|I\triangle J|\geq s/2\) for distinct \(I,J\in X\) and \(\log|X|\gtrsim s\log(n/s)\). The unit vectors \(x_I:=s^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in I}e_i\) lie in \(U_s\) and satisfy \[
\|x_I-x_J\|_2^2=\frac{|I\triangle J|}s\geq\frac12 ,
\] so they form a \(2^{-1/2}\)-separated subset of \(U_s\), and \(\log N(U_s,\tfrac12)\geq\log|X|\gtrsim s\log(n/s)\). Sudakov’s minoration with \(\varepsilon=\frac12\) gives \(w(U_s)\geq c\sqrt{s\log(n/s)}\), and \(\log(n/s)\asymp\log(en/s)\) in the stated range.



The lower bound is a first instance of Sudakov’s inequality being sharp: the entropy at the single scale \(\varepsilon=\frac12\) already accounts for the whole width. Compare the \(\ell^p\) balls of Lecture 12, where Sudakov is sharp at \(p=1\) and far from sharp for \(p>2\).

title: Lecture 13: Gaussian Width Revisited
text:
2 Random projections of sets
Let \(G\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix with independent \(N(0,1)\) entries and let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be bounded. The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma of Lecture 6 says that if \(T\) is finite and \(m\gtrsim\log|T|\), then \(G/\sqrt m\) acts on \(T\) as an approximate isometry, so in particular \(\operatorname{diam}(GT)\approx\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)\). For \(T=B_2^n\) nothing of the kind can hold when \(m<n\), since then \(\operatorname{diam}(GB_2^n)=2\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\approx2(\sqrt m+\sqrt n)\) is dominated by \(\sqrt n\), a quantity that does not shrink with \(m\). What happens in between is decided by the Gaussian width.

Theorem 1 (Diameter of a random projection) There are absolute constants \(c,C>0\) such that, for every bounded \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every \(m\geq1\), \[
c\big(w(T)+\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)\big)
\leq\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)
\leq C\big(w(T)+\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)\big).
\] Moreover, with probability at least \(1-e^{-m}\), \[
\operatorname{diam}(GT)\leq4w(T)+C\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T).
\]







NoteProof





Write \(D=\operatorname{diam}(T)\) and \(T'=T-T\), so that \(\sup_{x\in T'}\|x\|_2=D\) and \(w(T')=2w(T)\).
Upper bound, reduction to a net. For \(z\in\mathbb R^m\) define \[
\varphi(z):=\sup_{x\in T'}\langle Gx,z\rangle=\sup_{x\in T'}\langle G^{\mathsf T}z,x\rangle ,
\] so that \[
\operatorname{diam}(GT)=\sup_{x\in T'}\|Gx\|_2=\sup_{z\in S^{m-1}}\varphi(z).
\] Since \(T'\) is symmetric, \(\varphi\) is a seminorm on \(\mathbb R^m\), and the net argument of Lecture 8 applies to it: if \(N\) is a \(\frac12\)-net of \(S^{m-1}\) then \(\varphi(z)\leq\varphi(y)+\varphi(z-y)\leq\max_N\varphi+\frac12\sup_{S^{m-1}}\varphi\) for a net point \(y\) within \(\frac12\) of \(z\), hence \[
\sup_{z\in S^{m-1}}\varphi(z)\leq2\max_{y\in N}\varphi(y),
\qquad|N|\leq6^m .
\]
Upper bound, one direction. Fix \(y\in S^{m-1}\). By rotation invariance, \(G^{\mathsf T}y\sim N(0,I_n)\), so \[
\mathbb E\varphi(y)=\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T'}\langle G^{\mathsf T}y,x\rangle=w(T')=2w(T).
\] As a function of the \(mn\) Gaussian entries of \(G\), \(\varphi(y)\) is a supremum of linear functions and hence Lipschitz with constant \[
\sup_{x\in T'}\|xy^{\mathsf T}\|_F=\sup_{x\in T'}\|x\|_2=D ,
\] because \(\langle Gx,y\rangle=\langle G,yx^{\mathsf T}\rangle_F\). Gaussian concentration (Lecture 11) gives, for \(u\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\{\varphi(y)\geq2w(T)+u\}\leq e^{-u^2/(2D^2)}.
\]
Upper bound, union bound. Over the net, \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\max_{y\in N}\varphi(y)\geq2w(T)+u\Big\}\leq6^me^{-u^2/(2D^2)}\leq e^{-m}
\] once \(u=C_0\sqrt m\,D\) with \(C_0^2/2\geq1+\log6\). On the complementary event, \(\operatorname{diam}(GT)\leq2(2w(T)+C_0\sqrt mD)\), which is the high-probability claim. The bound in expectation follows by integrating the tail: for \(u\geq C_0\sqrt mD\) the same computation gives \(\mathbb P\{\operatorname{diam}(GT)\geq4w(T)+2u\}\leq6^me^{-u^2/(2D^2)}\), and \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\leq4w(T)+2C_0\sqrt mD+2\int_{C_0\sqrt mD}^\infty6^me^{-u^2/(2D^2)}\,du
\leq4w(T)+C\sqrt mD .
\]
Lower bound. Two different pairs of points witness the two terms. For the width, restrict attention to the first coordinate of \(Gx\): the first row \(G_1\) of \(G\) is \(N(0,I_n)\), and \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)=\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T'}\|Gx\|_2
\geq\mathbb E\sup_{x\in T'}\langle G_1,x\rangle=w(T')=2w(T).
\] For the diameter, fix \(x\in T'\). Then \(Gx\sim N(0,\|x\|_2^2I_m)\), so by Lecture 3 \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\geq\mathbb E\|Gx\|_2=\|x\|_2\,\mathbb E\|h\|_2\geq c_1\sqrt m\,\|x\|_2 ,
\qquad h\sim N(0,I_m),
\] and taking the supremum over \(x\in T'\) gives \(\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\geq c_1\sqrt mD\). Averaging the two lower bounds gives the claim with \(c=\min\{1,c_1\}/2\).



The proof has the same shape as the sharp bound on \(\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) in Lecture 12, and indeed \(T=B_2^n\) recovers it up to constants. There the supremum over the sphere \(S^{n-1}\) was handled by comparison; here the supremum over the general set \(T'\) is handled by concentration around the width, and only the supremum over the target sphere \(S^{m-1}\) needs a net. The net costs \(6^m\), which is exactly what makes \(\sqrt m\) the price of the target dimension.

2.1 The phase transition
Write the theorem as \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\asymp\max\Big\{w(T),\ \sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)\Big\}.
\] The two terms balance when \(m\asymp w(T)^2/\operatorname{diam}(T)^2\).

Definition 1 (Stable dimension) The stable dimension of a bounded set \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is \[
d(T):=\frac{w(T)^2}{\operatorname{diam}(T)^2}.
\]

In these terms:

If \(m\gtrsim d(T)\), then \(\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\asymp\sqrt m\operatorname{diam}(T)\). The projection behaves like the scaled isometry \(\sqrt m\cdot I\) on the diameter of \(T\), as it does for a finite set in the Johnson–Lindenstrauss regime.
If \(m\lesssim d(T)\), then \(\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(GT)\asymp w(T)\). The image is no smaller than the width of \(T\) no matter how few dimensions are kept. Projecting into fewer than \(d(T)\) dimensions does not compress the set any further.

The name is justified by two facts. First, \(d(T)\leq\dim T\), where \(\dim T\) is the dimension of the affine span of \(T\): if \(T\) lies in a \(k\)-dimensional subspace, then \(T-T\) lies in \(\operatorname{diam}(T)\cdot B_2^k\) up to a rotation, so \(2w(T)=w(T-T)\leq\operatorname{diam}(T)\,\mathbb E\|g'\|_2\leq\operatorname{diam}(T)\sqrt k\) with \(g'\sim N(0,I_k)\), and \(d(T)\leq k/4\). Second, \(d(T)\) is stable under perturbation of \(T\) in a way that the algebraic dimension is not: shrinking one axis of \(B_2^n\) to zero drops \(\dim\) from \(n\) to \(n-1\) only at the last instant, while \(d\) decreases continuously. For a finite set, \(d(T)\lesssim\log|T|\) by the finite-set bound of Lecture 3, which is the Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension again.






NoteOrthogonal projections





The theorem is stated for a Gaussian matrix, which is not a projection. If \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto a uniformly random \(m\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(\|Px\|_2\) has the law of \(\|Qx\|_2\), where \(Q\) consists of the first \(m\) rows of a Haar-distributed orthogonal matrix. The rows of \(Q\) are orthonormal, while the rows of \(G/\sqrt n\) are only approximately so; running the proof above with \(Q\) in place of \(G\), and using the spherical concentration inequality of Lecture 11 in place of the Gaussian one, gives \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{diam}(PT)\asymp\frac{w(T)}{\sqrt n}+\sqrt{\frac mn}\operatorname{diam}(T),
\] with the same phase transition at \(m\asymp d(T)\). The quantity \(w(T)/\sqrt n\) is the spherical width of \(T\), the expected width in a uniformly random direction. We do not carry out the reduction here.

title: Lecture 13: Gaussian Width Revisited
text:
3 Overlap of random cones
The second application replaces sets by cones and projection by rotation. A closed convex cone is a closed convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for all \(\lambda\geq0\). Let \(Q\) be a Haar distributed random orthogonal matrix, so that \(QC\) is a uniformly random rotation of a cone \(C\). Two cones in general position intersect only at the origin if they are small, and along a nontrivial set if they are large. The question is what “small” and “large” mean, and the answer is a width.

Lemma 1 (Projection onto a cone) Let \(C\) be a closed convex cone and let \(\Pi_C(x)\) denote the nearest point of \(C\) to \(x\). Then \[
\|\Pi_C(x)\|_2=\sup_{y\in C,\ \|y\|_2\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle .
\]







NoteProof





Write \(p=\Pi_C(x)\). The nearest-point characterization for a closed convex set gives \(\langle x-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\). Taking \(y=2p\) and \(y=0\), both in \(C\) because \(C\) is a cone, gives \(\langle x-p,p\rangle=0\), and then \(\langle x-p,y\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C\). Hence for \(y\in C\) with \(\|y\|_2\leq1\), \[
\langle y,x\rangle=\langle y,p\rangle+\langle y,x-p\rangle\leq\langle y,p\rangle\leq\|p\|_2 ,
\] with equality at \(y=p/\|p\|_2\) when \(p\neq0\). If \(p=0\) both sides vanish.




Definition 2 (Statistical dimension) The statistical dimension of a closed convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is \[
\delta(C):=\mathbb E\|\Pi_C(g)\|_2^2=\mathbb E\Big(\sup_{y\in C\cap B_2^n}\langle y,g\rangle\Big)^2 .
\]

This is a squared Gaussian width, up to an additive constant.

Lemma 2 (Statistical dimension and width) For every closed convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[
w(C\cap B_2^n)^2\leq\delta(C)\leq\big(w(C\cap B_2^n)+2\big)^2 .
\]







NoteProof





Let \(Z=\sup_{y\in C\cap B_2^n}\langle y,g\rangle\), so \(\mathbb EZ=w(C\cap B_2^n)\) and \(\delta(C)=\mathbb EZ^2\). The lower bound is Jensen. For the upper bound, \(Z\) is the support function of a set of radius \(1\), hence \(1\)-Lipschitz in \(g\), and Gaussian concentration (Lecture 11) gives \[
\operatorname{Var}Z=\int_0^\infty2t\,\mathbb P\{|Z-\mathbb EZ|\geq t\}\,dt
\leq\int_0^\infty4te^{-t^2/2}\,dt=4 .
\] Hence \(\mathbb EZ^2=\operatorname{Var}Z+(\mathbb EZ)^2\leq(\mathbb EZ)^2+4\leq(\mathbb EZ+2)^2\). The Gaussian Poincaré inequality, which we do not prove, gives \(\operatorname{Var}Z\leq1\) and hence the sharper bound \((w(C\cap B_2^n)+1)^2\).



Some examples. A linear subspace \(E\) of dimension \(k\) is a cone with \(\delta(E)=\mathbb E\|\Pi_Eg\|_2^2=k\), so statistical dimension extends linear dimension. The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb R^n_{\geq0}\) has \(\Pi(g)=(g_i^+)_i\) and \(\delta=n/2\). A circular cone of half-angle \(\theta\) has \(\delta\approx n\sin^2\theta\). In each case \(\delta(C)\) is the dimension of the subspace that the cone most resembles.

Theorem 2 (Approximate kinematic formula) There is an absolute constant \(C\) such that for all closed convex cones \(K,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), all \(\eta\in(0,1)\), and \(Q\) Haar orthogonal, \[
\delta(K)+\delta(C)\leq n-C\sqrt{n\log(1/\eta)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P\{K\cap QC\neq\{0\}\}\leq\eta ,
\] \[
\delta(K)+\delta(C)\geq n+C\sqrt{n\log(1/\eta)}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P\{K\cap QC\neq\{0\}\}\geq1-\eta .
\]

This is due to Amelunxen, Lotz, McCoy and Tropp (Amelunxen et al. 2014), and we state it without proof. Its content is that a randomly rotated pair of cones behaves like a pair of subspaces of dimensions \(\delta(K)\) and \(\delta(C)\). Two subspaces in general position intersect nontrivially if and only if their dimensions add up to more than \(n\), and the theorem says the same is true of cones, with statistical dimension in place of dimension and a transition window of width \(\sqrt n\) around the threshold. Since the window is of order \(\sqrt n\) while the dimensions are of order \(n\), the transition is sharp: for a family of cones with \((\delta(K)+\delta(C))/n\to\rho\), the intersection is trivial with probability tending to \(1\) if \(\rho<1\) and nontrivial with probability tending to \(1\) if \(\rho>1\).

Amelunxen, Dennis, Martin Lotz, Michael B. McCoy, and Joel A. Tropp. 2014. “Living on the Edge: Phase Transitions in Convex Programs with Random Data.” Information and Inference 3 (3): 224–94. https://doi.org/10.1093/imaiai/iau005.






NotePreview: the phase transition of sparse recovery





Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) Gaussian matrix and let \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\) be \(s\)-sparse. Basis pursuit recovers \(x_0\) from \(y=Ax_0\) as the minimizer of \(\|x\|_1\) subject to \(Ax=y\). The recovery succeeds exactly when the kernel of \(A\), a uniformly random subspace of dimension \(n-m\), meets the descent cone of the \(\ell^1\) norm at \(x_0\), \[
D(x_0):=\{h:\|x_0+\tau h\|_1\leq\|x_0\|_1\text{ for some }\tau>0\},
\] only at the origin. The kernel is a cone with \(\delta=n-m\), and a computation gives \(\delta(D(x_0))\approx2s\log(n/s)\) for \(s\ll n\). So the theorem predicts that basis pursuit succeeds with high probability when \(m\gtrsim2s\log(n/s)\) and fails with high probability when \(m\lesssim2s\log(n/s)\), with a transition window of width \(\sqrt n\). This is the empirically observed phase transition of compressed sensing, and it is a statement about the Gaussian width of a descent cone. We return to sparse recovery near the end of the course.

title: Lecture 13: Gaussian Width Revisited
text:
4 Where we go next
Gaussian width has now appeared in three roles: as the expected supremum of a Gaussian process, which is what the comparison inequalities compute; as a geometric size that controls covering numbers through Sudakov’s minoration; and as the parameter that governs random projections and random cones. The next two lectures leave Gaussian processes for a different use of Gaussian vectors, rounding the solution of a semidefinite program to a point of the discrete cube, before the course returns to suprema of processes with Dudley’s inequality and chaining.

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
text: Lecture 14 ended with a question. The semidefinite relaxation of a quadratic problem over the cube replaces signs by unit vectors in a Hilbert space, and rounding by a random hyperplane turns the inner products \(\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) into \(\frac2\pi\arcsin\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\). For max-cut the nonlinearity cost a factor \(0.878\). For a general bilinear form the nonlinearity has no sign to work with, and it is not clear that the relaxation is within any constant factor of the original problem. Grothendieck’s inequality says that it is. The proof given here, due to Krivine, removes the nonlinearity outright: it replaces the vectors by new vectors in a larger Hilbert space whose inner products have exactly the arcsine that the rounding produces. The Gaussian vector used to round then lives in an infinite-dimensional space, and it is the isonormal process of Lecture 10.

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
text:
1 The inequality

Theorem 1 (Grothendieck’s inequality) There is an absolute constant \(K\) with the following property. Let \(A=(A_{ij})\) be a real \(m\times n\) matrix such that \[
\Big|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}x_iy_j\Big|\leq1
\qquad\text{for all }x\in\{-1,1\}^m,\ y\in\{-1,1\}^n .
\] Then for every real Hilbert space \(H\) and all unit vectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n\in H\), \[
\Big|\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle\Big|\leq K .
\]

The smallest constant for which this holds is Grothendieck’s constant \(K_G\). Its exact value is unknown. Krivine’s argument below gives \[
K_G\leq\frac\pi{2\log(1+\sqrt2)}\approx1.782 ,
\] and it is known that \(K_G\geq1.676\) and that Krivine’s bound is not sharp.
The inequality would be trivial if \(K\) were allowed to depend on \(A\): the constant \(\sum_{ij}|A_{ij}|\) works, since \(|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|\leq1\). The content is that one constant serves for all matrices and all dimensions. Before the proof, three reformulations.

Lemma 1 (Equivalent forms)  

The hypothesis is equivalent to \(\big|\sum_{ij}A_{ij}x_iy_j\big|\leq\max_i|x_i|\cdot\max_j|y_j|\) for all real \(x\in\mathbb R^m\), \(y\in\mathbb R^n\).
The conclusion is equivalent to \(\big|\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle\big|\leq K\max_i\|u_i\|\cdot\max_j\|v_j\|\) for all vectors \(u_i,v_j\in H\), not necessarily of unit length.
It suffices to prove the conclusion for \(H=\mathbb R^{m+n}\).








NoteProof






By homogeneity it suffices to consider \(x\in[-1,1]^m\) and \(y\in[-1,1]^n\). For fixed \(y\), the map \(x\mapsto\sum_{ij}A_{ij}x_iy_j\) is linear, so its maximum and minimum over the cube \([-1,1]^m\) are attained at vertices, that is, at \(x\in\{-1,1\}^m\). Repeating the argument in \(y\) reduces to \(y\in\{-1,1\}^n\).
By homogeneity, suppose \(\|u_i\|\leq1\) and \(\|v_j\|\leq1\). Enlarge \(H\) to \(H\oplus\mathbb R^m\) with orthonormal vectors \(e'_1,\ldots,e'_m\) orthogonal to \(H\), and set \[
u'_i:=u_i\oplus\sqrt{1-\|u_i\|^2}\,e'_i,
\qquad
v'_j:=v_j\oplus0 .
\] Then \(\|u'_i\|=1\), \(\langle u'_i,v'_j\rangle=\langle u_i,v_j\rangle\), and the same device applied to the \(v_j\) with a further \(\mathbb R^n\) makes all vectors unit without changing any of the inner products.
The vectors \(u_i,v_j\) span a subspace of \(H\) of dimension at most \(m+n\), which is isometric to a subspace of \(\mathbb R^{m+n}\), and the inequality only involves inner products among them.

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
section: 2 What it says about semidefinite relaxations
text:
2 What it says about semidefinite relaxations
Define the bilinear integer and relaxed problems \[
\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A):=\max_{x\in\{\pm1\}^m,\ y\in\{\pm1\}^n}\sum_{ij}A_{ij}x_iy_j,
\qquad
\mathrm{SDP}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A):=\max_{\substack{u_i,v_j\in S^{m+n-1}}}\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle .
\] Both maxima are nonnegative, since replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) flips the sign, and the second is a semidefinite program by the Gram-matrix lemma of Lecture 14, applied to the \(m+n\) vectors together. The integer value \(\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\) is the cut norm of \(A\), up to a constant factor, and computing it is NP-hard.

Corollary 1 (The bilinear relaxation is tight up to \(K_G\)) For every real \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\), \[
\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\leq\mathrm{SDP}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\leq K_G\cdot\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A).
\]







NoteProof





The first inequality takes \(u_i=x_ie_1\), \(v_j=y_je_1\). For the second, if \(\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)=0\) then \(A=0\) and there is nothing to prove; otherwise apply Theorem 1 to \(A/\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\), which satisfies the hypothesis.



So the bilinear relaxation computes the cut norm to within a factor \(K_G<1.79\) in polynomial time, and with more work the relaxed solution can be rounded to sign vectors achieving a constant fraction of the optimum (Alon and Naor 2006). This is what the hyperplane rounding of Lecture 14 could not do for general coefficients.

Alon, Noga, and Assaf Naor. 2006. “Approximating the Cut-Norm via Grothendieck’s Inequality.” SIAM Journal on Computing 35 (4): 787–803. https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539704441629.

Alon, Noga, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev, and Assaf Naor. 2006. “Quadratic Forms on Graphs.” Inventiones Mathematicae 163 (3): 499–522. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-005-0465-9.
The symmetric problem of Lecture 14 is different. For a symmetric \(A\) with zero diagonal, polarization relates the two: \[
\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle Au,u\rangle-\langle Av,v\rangle,
\qquad u=\frac{x+y}2,\ v=\frac{x-y}2 .
\] For \(x,y\in\{-1,1\}^n\) the vectors \(u,v\) lie in \([-1,1]^n\), and a quadratic form with zero diagonal is linear in each variable separately, so its maximum and minimum over \([-1,1]^n\) are attained on the cube. Hence \(\mathrm{INT}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\leq\mathrm{INT}(A)+\mathrm{INT}(-A)\leq2\max_x|\langle Ax,x\rangle|\), and since the symmetric relaxation is the bilinear one restricted to \(u_i=v_i\), \[
\mathrm{SDP}(A)\leq\mathrm{SDP}_{\mathrm{bil}}(A)\leq2K_G\max_{x\in\{\pm1\}^n}|\langle Ax,x\rangle| .
\] The absolute value cannot be removed. Alon, Makarychev, Makarychev and Naor (Alon et al. 2006) showed that the ratio \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)/\mathrm{INT}(A)\) can be as large as \(c\log n\) for symmetric \(A\) with zero diagonal, and that \(C\log n\) is the worst case. So the constant-factor guarantee is a genuinely bilinear phenomenon: letting \(x\) and \(y\) vary independently is what makes the relaxation tight. For max-cut the issue does not arise, because the Goemans–Williamson analysis works directly with the objective \(1-\langle X_i,X_j\rangle\) and never needs a comparison of \(\mathrm{SDP}(A)\) with \(\mathrm{INT}(A)\).

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
text:
3 Krivine’s proof
By Lemma 1 we may assume \(H=\mathbb R^d\) with \(d=m+n\) and all \(u_i,v_j\) of unit length. The proof has two ideas, which the handwritten notes label as follows.
Idea 1. Find a Hilbert space \(\widehat H\) and maps \(\Phi,\Psi\) from the unit sphere of \(H\) to the unit sphere of \(\widehat H\) such that \[
\frac2\pi\arcsin\big\langle\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\big\rangle=\beta\langle u,v\rangle
\qquad\text{for all unit }u,v\in H,
\tag{1}\] for some constant \(\beta>0\).
Idea 2. Round with the isonormal process on \(\widehat H\). Grothendieck’s identity turns the left side of Equation 1 into an expectation of a product of signs, and the hypothesis on \(A\) bounds the expectation pointwise.
We carry out Idea 2 first, assuming Idea 1, and then construct \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\).






NoteProof of the theorem, given Idea 1





Let \(\Phi,\Psi,\beta\) be as in Equation 1, and let \(g\) be the isonormal process on \(\widehat H\) from Lecture 10. For unit vectors \(h,h'\in\widehat H\), the pair \((g(h),g(h'))\) is centered Gaussian with unit variances and covariance \(\langle h,h'\rangle\), which is also the law of \((\langle\gamma,a\rangle,\langle\gamma,b\rangle)\) for \(\gamma\sim N(0,I_2)\) and unit \(a,b\in\mathbb R^2\) with \(\langle a,b\rangle=\langle h,h'\rangle\). Grothendieck’s identity of Lecture 14 depends only on this joint law, so \[
\mathbb E\operatorname{sgn}g(h)\operatorname{sgn}g(h')=\frac2\pi\arcsin\langle h,h'\rangle .
\] Apply this with \(h=\Phi(u_i)\) and \(h'=\Psi(v_j)\), and use Equation 1: \[
\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle
=\frac1\beta\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\,\frac2\pi\arcsin\langle\Phi(u_i),\Psi(v_j)\rangle
=\frac1\beta\,\mathbb E\Big[\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\,\operatorname{sgn}g(\Phi(u_i))\operatorname{sgn}g(\Psi(v_j))\Big].
\] For every outcome, \(x_i:=\operatorname{sgn}g(\Phi(u_i))\) and \(y_j:=\operatorname{sgn}g(\Psi(v_j))\) are sign vectors, so the bracket is at most \(1\) in absolute value by hypothesis. Hence \(\big|\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle\big|\leq1/\beta\), which is the theorem with \(K=1/\beta\).



Note where the isonormal process earned its keep. The vectors \(\Phi(u_i)\) and \(\Psi(v_j)\) will live in an infinite-dimensional space, and the Gaussian process indexed by that space is exactly what makes “round with a random hyperplane” meaningful there. Since only finitely many vectors are involved, one could restrict to their span and use an ordinary Gaussian vector; the isonormal process simply avoids having to say so.

3.1 The kernel trick
The construction behind Idea 1 represents a nonlinear function of an inner product as a linear inner product in a bigger space. For \(H=\mathbb R^d\) and \(k\geq1\), the \(k\)-th tensor power of a vector \(u\in\mathbb R^d\) is the array \[
u^{\otimes k}:=\big(u_{i_1}u_{i_2}\cdots u_{i_k}\big)_{1\leq i_1,\ldots,i_k\leq d}\in\mathbb R^{d^k},
\] and with the standard inner product on \(\mathbb R^{d^k}\), \[
\langle u^{\otimes k},v^{\otimes k}\rangle
=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}\prod_{\ell=1}^ku_{i_\ell}v_{i_\ell}
=\Big(\sum_iu_iv_i\Big)^k=\langle u,v\rangle^k .
\tag{2}\] So the monomial \(t\mapsto t^k\) is realized as an inner product in \(\mathbb R^{d^k}\). Sums of monomials are realized in direct sums of these spaces. For Hilbert spaces \(H_1,H_2,\ldots\) the direct sum \(\bigoplus_kH_k\) is the space of sequences \((h_k)_k\) with \(h_k\in H_k\) and \(\sum_k\|h_k\|^2<\infty\), with inner product \(\langle(h_k),(h'_k)\rangle=\sum_k\langle h_k,h'_k\rangle\); it is a separable Hilbert space when each \(H_k\) is.

Lemma 2 (The kernel trick) Let \(f(t)=\sum_{k\geq1}a_kt^k\) be a power series with \(\sum_k|a_k|\leq1\). Let \(\widehat H:=\bigoplus_{k\geq1}\mathbb R^{d^k}\) and define, for \(u,v\in\mathbb R^d\) with \(\|u\|,\|v\|\leq1\), \[
\Phi(u):=\big(\operatorname{sgn}(a_k)\sqrt{|a_k|}\,u^{\otimes k}\big)_{k\geq1},
\qquad
\Psi(v):=\big(\sqrt{|a_k|}\,v^{\otimes k}\big)_{k\geq1}.
\] Then \(\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\in\widehat H\), and \[
\langle\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\rangle=f(\langle u,v\rangle),
\qquad
\|\Phi(u)\|^2=\|\Psi(u)\|^2=\sum_{k\geq1}|a_k|\,\|u\|^{2k}.
\] In particular \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) map unit vectors to vectors of norm \(\big(\sum_k|a_k|\big)^{1/2}\leq1\), with equality when \(\sum_k|a_k|=1\).







NoteProof





By Equation 2, \(\|u^{\otimes k}\|^2=\|u\|^{2k}\leq1\), so \(\sum_k|a_k|\|u\|^{2k}\leq\sum_k|a_k|<\infty\) and \(\Phi(u)\in\widehat H\); likewise for \(\Psi\). The inner product is \[
\langle\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\rangle=\sum_k\operatorname{sgn}(a_k)|a_k|\langle u^{\otimes k},v^{\otimes k}\rangle
=\sum_ka_k\langle u,v\rangle^k=f(\langle u,v\rangle),
\] the series converging absolutely since \(|\langle u,v\rangle|\leq1\). The norms are computed the same way with \(u=v\).



The signs of the coefficients are placed on \(\Phi\) only. This is why two different maps are needed: a single map \(\Phi=\Psi\) would represent only series with nonnegative coefficients, and the function we need has coefficients of both signs.


3.2 Krivine’s choice of \(f\)
Identity Equation 1 asks for \[
\langle\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\rangle=\sin\Big(\frac{\pi\beta}2\langle u,v\rangle\Big),
\] so we take \(f(t)=\sin(ct)\) with \(c=\pi\beta/2\). Its power series is \[
\sin(ct)=\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{(-1)^kc^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\,t^{2k+1},
\qquad
\sum_k|a_k|=\sum_{k\geq0}\frac{c^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}=\sinh c .
\] For Lemma 2 to send unit vectors to unit vectors we need \(\sinh c=1\), that is \[
c=\operatorname{arcsinh}(1)=\log\big(1+\sqrt2\big),
\qquad
\beta=\frac{2c}\pi=\frac2\pi\log\big(1+\sqrt2\big)\approx0.561 .
\] With this choice, for unit \(u,v\) the vectors \(\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\) are unit vectors in \(\widehat H\) with \(\langle\Phi(u),\Psi(v)\rangle=\sin(\frac{\pi\beta}2\langle u,v\rangle)\), and since \(|\frac{\pi\beta}2\langle u,v\rangle|\leq c<\pi/2\), taking the arcsine gives Equation 1. This completes Idea 1, and the theorem follows with \[
K=\frac1\beta=\frac\pi{2\log(1+\sqrt2)}\approx1.782 .
\]
The handwritten notes leave \(\beta\) unspecified; the computation above is the only place where a number enters. Larger \(\beta\) would give a better constant, and the constraint \(\sinh(\pi\beta/2)\leq1\) is exactly the requirement that the kernel trick produce unit vectors. Whether a cleverer choice of \(f\), or a cleverer rounding, can do better is the question of the exact value of \(K_G\).






NoteA second proof, with a worse constant





It is instructive to see that \(K_G<\infty\) can be proved without the kernel trick, by Gaussian realization and truncation. Fix \(A\) satisfying the hypothesis and let \(K(A)\) be the best constant in the conclusion over all Hilbert spaces, which is finite. Choose unit vectors realizing it, so \(\sum_{ij}A_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle=K(A)\), and let \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), \(U_i=\langle g,u_i\rangle\), \(V_j=\langle g,v_j\rangle\). Then \(K(A)=\mathbb E\sum_{ij}A_{ij}U_iV_j\). If the \(U_i,V_j\) were bounded by \(R\), the hypothesis would give \(K(A)\leq R^2\) at once. They are not, so split \(U_i=U_i^-+U_i^+\) with \(U_i^-=U_i\mathbb 1\{|U_i|\leq R\}\), and likewise \(V_j\). The term with both bounded parts is at most \(R^2\). Each of the three remaining terms is a bilinear form in vectors of \(L^2(\mathbb P)\), a Hilbert space, and the definition of \(K(A)\) bounds it by \(K(A)\max\|U_i^\pm\|_{L^2}\max\|V_j^\pm\|_{L^2}\). A Gaussian tail computation gives \(\|U_i^+\|_{L^2}\leq2/R\) for \(R\geq1\), so \[
K(A)\leq R^2+\frac{6K(A)}R .
\] Taking \(R=12\) gives \(K(A)\leq288\), uniformly in \(A\). The argument shows where the difficulty lies: the Gaussian realization is exact, and all the loss is in handling the unbounded tails, which the sign rounding of Krivine’s proof avoids entirely.

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
text:
4 Kernels, feature maps, and history
The kernel trick is much older and much wider than this application. A function \(\kappa:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is a positive definite kernel if \((\kappa(x_i,x_j))_{ij}\) is positive semidefinite for every finite family of points, and the Moore–Aronszajn theorem says that these are exactly the functions of the form \(\kappa(x,y)=\langle\Phi(x),\Phi(y)\rangle\) for a map \(\Phi\) into some Hilbert space, the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of \(\kappa\). In machine learning one chooses a kernel, such as \(\exp(-\|x-y\|^2/2\sigma^2)\) or \((\langle x,y\rangle+r)^k\), and runs a linear algorithm in the feature space without ever writing \(\Phi\) down, since only inner products are needed. Krivine’s argument runs in the other direction: the target function \(\sin(c\langle u,v\rangle)\) is not a positive definite kernel, because its series has coefficients of both signs, and the two maps \(\Phi\neq\Psi\) are what handle the negative ones.
Grothendieck proved the inequality in 1953 (Grothendieck 1953), in the language of tensor norms and with the constant \(\sinh(\pi/2)\approx2.30\). Krivine’s proof and constant date from 1979 (Krivine 1979). Braverman, Makarychev, Makarychev and Naor (Braverman et al. 2013) showed that Krivine’s bound is not the true value of \(K_G\), though no explicit better constant is known. Pisier’s survey (Pisier 2012) traces the inequality through functional analysis, operator algebras, and computer science.

Grothendieck, Alexandre. 1953. “Résumé de La Théorie Métrique Des Produits Tensoriels Topologiques.” Boletim Da Sociedade de Matemática de São Paulo 8: 1–79.

Krivine, Jean-Louis. 1979. “Constantes de Grothendieck Et Fonctions de Type Positif Sur Les Sphères.” Advances in Mathematics 31 (1): 16–30.

Braverman, Mark, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev, and Assaf Naor. 2013. “The Grothendieck Constant Is Strictly Smaller Than Krivine’s Bound.” Forum of Mathematics, Pi 1: e4. https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2013.4.

Pisier, Gilles. 2012. “Grothendieck’s Theorem, Past and Present.” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 49 (2): 237–323. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-2011-01348-9.

title: Lecture 15: Grothendieck’s Inequality
text:
5 Where we go next
The convex relaxation detour is over. The course returns to suprema of Gaussian and sub-Gaussian processes, this time from the upper side: the next lecture proves Dudley’s inequality, which bounds \(\mathbb E\sup X\) by an integral of the metric entropy of the index set over all scales, and introduces chaining, the technique that will occupy the rest of the term.

title: Lecture 17: Applications of Dudley’s Inequality
text: Dudley’s inequality asks nothing of a process beyond sub-Gaussian increments and a metric with computable covering numbers. This lecture exploits that generality in two directions. The first is statistical: the empirical average of a function class, over all functions in the class at once, is close to the true average, and the price of uniformity is an entropy integral over the class. The second is analytic: a process whose increments are Hölder in the \(\psi_2\) norm has Hölder continuous sample paths, and the exponent lost in the passage is as small as one likes. Brownian motion is the canonical example of both the hypothesis and the conclusion.

title: Lecture 17: Applications of Dudley’s Inequality
text:
1 Empirical processes
Let \(Y,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be i.i.d. random variables with values in a set \(\mathcal Y\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions \(f:\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R\). The law of large numbers says that for each fixed \(f\), \[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)\longrightarrow\mathbb Ef(Y).
\] A uniform law of large numbers for \(\mathcal F\) is a bound on \[
\mathbb E\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Big|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\Big| .
\] Such bounds are the basic tool of statistical learning: a learning algorithm chooses \(f\) after seeing the data, so the ordinary law of large numbers, which fixes \(f\) in advance, does not apply to the chosen \(f\). A uniform bound does.
The centered and normalized process \[
X_f:=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(f(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\big),
\qquad f\in\mathcal F,
\] is called the empirical process indexed by \(\mathcal F\).

Lemma 1 (The empirical process is sub-Gaussian) For all \(f,g\in\mathcal F\) with \(\|f-g\|_\infty<\infty\), \[
\|X_f-X_g\|_{\psi_2}\leq2\|f-g\|_\infty .
\] So the empirical process is sub-Gaussian with respect to the metric \(d(f,g)=2\|f-g\|_\infty\).







NoteProof





Write \(h=f-g\). Then \(X_f-X_g=n^{-1/2}\sum_i(h(Y_i)-\mathbb Eh(Y))\) is a sum of \(n\) independent, mean-zero variables, each taking values in an interval of length at most \(2\|h\|_\infty\). By Hoeffding’s lemma of Lecture 4 each summand is \(\|h\|_\infty^2\)-subgaussian, so by the Pythagorean theorem of Lecture 5 the sum is \(n\|h\|_\infty^2\)-subgaussian, and after dividing by \(\sqrt n\) the increment is \(\|h\|_\infty^2\)-subgaussian. The sub-Gaussian–\(\psi_2\) comparison of Lecture 5 gives the claim.



Dudley’s inequality now applies verbatim.

Theorem 1 (Uniform law of large numbers via entropy) Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions that is bounded and separable in the supremum norm. Then \[
\mathbb E\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Big|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\Big|
\leq\frac C{\sqrt n}\Big[\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon+\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\|f\|_\infty\Big].
\]







NoteProof





Fix \(f_0\in\mathcal F\). By Lemma 1 and the tail form of Dudley’s inequality (Lecture 16), integrated in \(u\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|X_f-X_{f_0}|\leq C\int_0^\infty\sqrt{\log N(\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon ,
\] where the factor \(2\) in the metric has been absorbed into \(C\). The base point contributes \(\mathbb E|X_{f_0}|\leq(\mathbb EX_{f_0}^2)^{1/2}\leq\|f_0\|_\infty\). Adding the two and dividing by \(\sqrt n\) gives the claim, since the empirical average deviation is \(X_f/\sqrt n\).



The theorem separates two effects. The factor \(n^{-1/2}\) is the rate of the ordinary law of large numbers, and the bracket is the price of uniformity, a fixed number depending only on the class. The next example computes the price for a natural class.

1.1 Lipschitz functions on an interval
Let \(Y\) take values in \([0,1]\) and let \[
\mathcal F_L:=\big\{f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R:\ \|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\leq L\big\}.
\] Adding a constant to \(f\) does not change the deviation \(\frac1n\sum_if(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\), so we may restrict to \(f(0)=0\), which forces \(\|f\|_\infty\leq L\).

Lemma 2 (Entropy of Lipschitz functions) Let \(\mathcal F_L^0:=\{f\in\mathcal F_L:f(0)=0\}\). Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[
\log N(\mathcal F_L^0,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)\leq\frac{CL}\varepsilon .
\]







NoteProof





By scaling, take \(L=1\). Fix \(\delta>0\) and the grid points \(x_k=k\delta\) for \(0\leq k\leq1/\delta\). Given \(f\in\mathcal F_1^0\), let \(g\) be the piecewise linear function on the grid whose value at \(x_k\) is the nearest point of \((\delta/2)\mathbb Z\) to \(f(x_k)\), with \(g(0)=0\). Then \(|g(x_k)-f(x_k)|\leq\delta/4\), and since \(|f(x_{k+1})-f(x_k)|\leq\delta\), the increment \(g(x_{k+1})-g(x_k)\) lies in \((\delta/2)\mathbb Z\) and has absolute value at most \(3\delta/2\), leaving \(7\) possibilities at each step. So there are at most \(7^{1/\delta}\) functions \(g\). For \(x\in[x_k,x_{k+1}]\), \[
|f(x)-g(x)|\leq|f(x)-f(x_k)|+|f(x_k)-g(x_k)|+|g(x_k)-g(x)|\leq\delta+\frac\delta4+\frac{3\delta}2\leq3\delta .
\] Thus \(\mathcal F_1^0\) is covered by \(7^{1/\delta}\) balls of radius \(3\delta\) centered at functions \(g\), which need not lie in \(\mathcal F_1^0\); replacing each center by a point of \(\mathcal F_1^0\) in its ball doubles the radius. Taking \(\varepsilon=6\delta\) gives \(\log N(\mathcal F_1^0,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)\leq(6\log7)/\varepsilon\).



The picture behind the proof is the one in the handwritten notes: a \(1\)-Lipschitz path through a grid of boxes of side \(\delta\) enters, at each step, one of a bounded number of neighboring boxes, and the path is determined up to \(O(\delta)\) by the sequence of boxes.

Corollary 1 (Uniform law of large numbers for Lipschitz functions) For every \(L>0\) and every \(n\geq1\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_L}\Big|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\Big|\leq\frac{CL}{\sqrt n}.
\]







NoteProof





Apply Theorem 1 to \(\mathcal F_L^0\), whose diameter in the supremum norm is at most \(2L\), so the entropy integral runs over \([0,2L]\): \[
\int_0^{2L}\sqrt{\frac{CL}\varepsilon}\,d\varepsilon=\sqrt{CL}\cdot2\sqrt{2L}=C'L ,
\qquad
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_L^0}\|f\|_\infty\leq L .
\]



So the empirical average of a Lipschitz function converges at the parametric rate \(n^{-1/2}\) uniformly over the whole class, with the Lipschitz constant as the only price. The entropy integral converged because \(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon}\) is integrable at \(0\): the class is “small” in exactly the sense that matters for Dudley.






NoteHigher dimensions, and the limits of the supremum norm





For Lipschitz functions on \([0,1]^d\) the same box-counting argument gives \(\log N(\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)\leq C_d/\varepsilon^d\), and \(\sqrt{\varepsilon^{-d}}\) is not integrable at \(0\) once \(d\geq2\). Dudley’s inequality then gives nothing, although the uniform law of large numbers is true, with the slower rate \(n^{-1/d}\) for \(d\geq3\). The supremum norm is the wrong metric: two functions that differ on a tiny region are far apart in \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) but produce nearly identical empirical averages. The right metric is the empirical \(L^2\) distance \[
d_n(f,g)^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(f(Y_i)-g(Y_i)\big)^2 ,
\] in which the increments are still sub-Gaussian conditionally on the sample, and the covering numbers are much smaller. Problem 1 of Exercise Sheet 4 is a first step in this direction: it shows that covering numbers in \(L^2\) of the population measure are preserved by sampling. Carrying this program through leads to the theory of Vapnik–Chervonenkis classes, which we do not develop.

title: Lecture 17: Applications of Dudley’s Inequality
text:
2 Continuity of sample paths
The second application uses Dudley’s inequality not for its numerical bound but for its uniformity in the index. A process indexed by an interval is a random function, and Dudley controls its oscillation over sub-intervals of every length at once.

Theorem 2 (Hölder continuity criterion) Let \((X_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) be a centered process and suppose there are \(\beta\in(0,1]\) and \(M>0\) such that \[
\|X_t-X_s\|_{\psi_2}\leq M|t-s|^\beta
\qquad\text{for all }s,t\in[0,1].
\] Then for every \(\alpha<\beta\) there is a constant \(C_{\alpha,\beta}\) such that \[
\mathbb E\sup_{s\neq t}\frac{|X_t-X_s|}{|t-s|^\alpha}\leq C_{\alpha,\beta}M ,
\] the supremum being over \(s,t\) in a countable dense subset of \([0,1]\). In particular \(X\) has a version with \(\alpha\)-Hölder continuous sample paths.







NoteProof





Take \(M=1\) by scaling, and let \(D\) be a countable dense subset of \([0,1]\) containing the dyadic rationals. The process is sub-Gaussian with respect to \(d(s,t)=|t-s|^\beta\).
Step 1: one dyadic interval. Let \(I\) be a dyadic interval of length \(2^{-k}\). Its \(d\)-diameter is \(2^{-k\beta}\), and \(N(I,d,\varepsilon)=N(I,|\cdot|,\varepsilon^{1/\beta})\leq2^{-k}\varepsilon^{-1/\beta}+1\). Substituting \(\varepsilon=2^{-k\beta}\eta\), \[
\int_0^{2^{-k\beta}}\sqrt{\log N(I,d,\varepsilon)}\,d\varepsilon
=2^{-k\beta}\int_0^1\sqrt{\log\big(\eta^{-1/\beta}+1\big)}\,d\eta
\leq C_\beta2^{-k\beta}.
\] By the tail form of Dudley’s inequality (Lecture 16) applied to the process on \(I\cap D\), for every \(v\geq0\), \[
\mathbb P\Big\{\sup_{s,t\in I\cap D}|X_t-X_s|\geq C_\beta2^{-k\beta}(1+v)\Big\}\leq2e^{-v^2}.
\]
Step 2: all dyadic intervals at once. There are \(2^k\) dyadic intervals of length \(2^{-k}\). Take \(v=v_k:=\sqrt{2k}+u\) with \(u\geq0\); then \(2^k\cdot2e^{-v_k^2}\leq2e^{-u^2}e^{-k}\), and summing over \(k\geq0\) the probability that some dyadic interval of some length violates its bound is at most \(4e^{-u^2}\).
Step 3: from dyadic intervals to all pairs. On the good event, let \(s<t\) in \(D\) and choose \(k\) with \(2^{-k-1}<t-s\leq2^{-k}\). The points \(s\) and \(t\) lie in the same or in two adjacent dyadic intervals of length \(2^{-k}\), so by the triangle inequality across the shared endpoint, \[
|X_t-X_s|\leq2C_\beta2^{-k\beta}\big(1+\sqrt{2k}+u\big)
\leq4C_\beta(t-s)^\beta\Big(1+\sqrt{2\log_2\tfrac1{t-s}}+u\Big).
\] Since \(\alpha<\beta\), \((t-s)^{\beta-\alpha}\sqrt{\log_2(1/(t-s))}\) is bounded on \((0,1]\) by a constant \(C'_{\alpha,\beta}\), and hence \[
\sup_{s\neq t}\frac{|X_t-X_s|}{|t-s|^\alpha}\leq C_{\alpha,\beta}(1+u)
\] with probability at least \(1-4e^{-u^2}\). Integrating in \(u\) gives the expectation bound.
Step 4: the version. On the almost sure event where the Hölder quotient is finite, \(t\mapsto X_t\) is uniformly continuous on \(D\) and so extends uniquely to an \(\alpha\)-Hölder function on \([0,1]\). Since \(X_{t_k}\to X_t\) in probability as \(t_k\to t\) by the increment hypothesis, the extension agrees with \(X_t\) almost surely at each \(t\), so it is a version of the process.



The proof is chaining at the level of intervals: Dudley handles each dyadic interval, and a union bound with a slowly growing \(v_k\) handles the scales. The loss from \(\beta\) to \(\alpha<\beta\) comes entirely from the \(\sqrt{\log}\) factor in Step 3, which is the cost of the union bound over \(2^k\) intervals. It cannot be removed in general, as the next example shows.

Corollary 2 (Brownian motion is Hölder continuous) Let \((B_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) be Brownian motion, the centered Gaussian process with covariance \(\min\{s,t\}\) from Lecture 10. Then \(B\) has a version whose sample paths are \(\alpha\)-Hölder continuous for every \(\alpha<\tfrac12\).







NoteProof





\(B_t-B_s\sim N(0,|t-s|)\), so \(\|B_t-B_s\|_{\psi_2}\leq2|t-s|^{1/2}\) by the sub-Gaussian–\(\psi_2\) comparison. Apply Theorem 2 with \(\beta=\tfrac12\) and every \(\alpha<\tfrac12\); a single version works for all \(\alpha\) by taking a sequence \(\alpha_j\uparrow\tfrac12\) and intersecting the almost sure events.



The exponent \(\tfrac12\) itself is not attained. Lévy’s modulus of continuity states that \[
\limsup_{h\downarrow0}\ \sup_{|t-s|\leq h}\frac{|B_t-B_s|}{\sqrt{2h\log(1/h)}}=1
\qquad\text{almost surely},
\] so the paths oscillate by \(\sqrt{2h\log(1/h)}\) over intervals of length \(h\), which is the bound of Step 3 with \(\beta=\tfrac12\) and the logarithm kept. Dudley’s argument, applied with care, is sharp for Brownian motion.






NoteThe Gaussian free field is not a function





The criterion is a statement about the growth of increments in the \(\psi_2\) norm. Consider the isonormal process on \(H=L^2[0,1]\) from Lecture 10 and the process \(X_t=g(\mathbb 1_{[0,t]})\): this is Brownian motion, and its increments satisfy \(\|X_t-X_s\|_{L^2}=|t-s|^{1/2}\). The two-dimensional Gaussian free field is the Gaussian process on a planar domain whose covariance kernel is \(-\log|t-s|\) up to a bounded function. The kernel diverges on the diagonal, so the variance at a point is infinite and there is no process \(X_t\) to which a criterion of this kind could apply: the field exists only after integrating against test functions, as a random distribution, exactly as the isonormal process \(g(h)\) exists for \(h\in L^2\) but \(g(\delta_t)\) does not. The Hölder criterion marks the boundary between processes that are random functions and processes that are not.

title: Lecture 17: Applications of Dudley’s Inequality
text:
3 Where we go next
Both applications used Dudley’s inequality as a black box, with the whole argument in the computation of covering numbers. The next two lectures return to the inequality itself. Dudley uses one net at each scale for every point of \(T\), and the Talagrand and \(\ell^1\)-ball examples of Lecture 16 showed that this is wasteful when the geometry of \(T\) varies from place to place. Generic chaining lets the nets adapt, and for Gaussian processes the resulting functional \(\gamma_2(T,d)\) is equivalent to \(\mathbb E\sup X\) up to absolute constants, closing the gap between Sudakov and Dudley.

title: Lecture 19: The Lower Bound and the Matrix Deviation Inequality
text: Lecture 18 stated the majorizing measure theorem and proved its upper half, the generic chaining bound \(\mathbb E\sup X\leq C\gamma_2(T,d)\). This lecture does two things with the lower half. It explains the mechanism of the proof, a tree of well-separated subsets of \(T\) along which Sudakov’s minoration is applied at every branching, and it uses the theorem in the form that matters for applications: any process with sub-Gaussian increments is dominated by the Gaussian process with the same increments. The application is the matrix deviation inequality, which controls \(\|Ax\|_2-\sqrt m\|x\|_2\) uniformly over an arbitrary set of vectors \(x\) by the Gaussian width of the set, for a matrix \(A\) with independent sub-Gaussian rows. It is the tool that Lecture 9 lacked.

title: Lecture 19: The Lower Bound and the Matrix Deviation Inequality
text:
1 Sudakov’s minoration with a remainder
The lower bound in Sudakov’s minoration (Lecture 12) says that \(\varepsilon\)-separated points force \(\mathbb E\sup X\geq c\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N}\). For an iterative argument one needs more: the separated points should carry subsets of \(T\), and the process should pay \(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N}\) in addition to whatever the subsets themselves force.

Lemma 1 (Sudakov with a remainder) There are absolute constants \(c,c'>0\) with the following property. Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) be a centered Gaussian process with canonical metric \(d\), and let \(T_1,\ldots,T_N\subseteq T\) be subsets, \(N\geq2\), such that \[
\operatorname{diam}(T_j)\leq c\,\varepsilon
\quad\text{for all }j,
\qquad
d(T_j,T_k)\geq\varepsilon
\quad\text{for all }j\neq k .
\] Then \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\geq c'\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N}+\min_{j\leq N}\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T_j}X_t .
\]







NoteProof





Let \(T'=\bigcup_jT_j\); it suffices to bound \(\mathbb E\sup_{T'}X\) from below. We build a comparison process. Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\) be i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\), and for each \(j\) let \((Z^{(j)}_t)_{t\in T_j}\) be an independent copy of the process \((X_t)_{t\in T_j}\), all independent of one another and of the \(g_j\). For \(t\in T_j\) define \[
Y_t:=\frac\varepsilon4g_j+Z^{(j)}_t .
\] We compare increments. For \(s,t\) in the same \(T_j\), \(\mathbb E(Y_t-Y_s)^2=\mathbb E(X_t-X_s)^2\). For \(t\in T_j\) and \(s\in T_k\) with \(j\neq k\), independence gives \[
\mathbb E(Y_t-Y_s)^2=\frac{\varepsilon^2}8+\mathbb E(Z^{(j)}_t)^2+\mathbb E(Z^{(k)}_s)^2
\leq\frac{\varepsilon^2}8+2c^2\varepsilon^2 ,
\] if we normalize so that the processes \(Z^{(j)}\) are centered at a point of \(T_j\), which changes nothing, so that \(\mathbb E(Z^{(j)}_t)^2\leq\operatorname{diam}(T_j)^2\leq c^2\varepsilon^2\); while \(\mathbb E(X_t-X_s)^2=d(t,s)^2\geq\varepsilon^2\). Choosing \(c\) small enough that \(\frac18+2c^2\leq1\) gives \(\mathbb E(Y_t-Y_s)^2\leq\mathbb E(X_t-X_s)^2\) for all \(s,t\in T'\). By the Sudakov–Fernique inequality of Lecture 12, \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T'}X_t\geq\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T'}Y_t
=\mathbb E\max_{j\leq N}\Big(\frac\varepsilon4g_j+\sup_{t\in T_j}Z^{(j)}_t\Big).
\] Condition on \(g_1,\ldots,g_N\). The suprema \(\sup_{T_j}Z^{(j)}\) are independent of the \(g_j\), and by Jensen’s inequality applied to the convex function \(\max_j\), replacing each of them by its expectation \(\mathbb E\sup_{T_j}X\) can only decrease the conditional expectation: \[
\mathbb E\max_j\Big(\frac\varepsilon4g_j+\sup_{T_j}Z^{(j)}\Big)
\geq\mathbb E\max_j\Big(\frac\varepsilon4g_j+\mathbb E\sup_{T_j}X\Big)
\geq\frac\varepsilon4\,\mathbb E\max_jg_j+\min_j\mathbb E\sup_{T_j}X .
\] Finally \(\mathbb E\max_{j\leq N}g_j\geq c_0\sqrt{\log N}\) for \(N\geq2\), as in the proof of Sudakov’s minoration.



The lemma is Sudakov’s minoration when the \(T_j\) are single points. The gain is the second term: whatever the process achieves inside the pieces is added to, not replaced by, the separation cost at the coarse scale. This is what allows the bound to be iterated down a tree of scales.

title: Lecture 19: The Lower Bound and the Matrix Deviation Inequality
text:
2 Trees and the lower bound
Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), a fixed ratio between consecutive scales; \(\alpha=\tfrac14\) will do. A tree on \(T\) is a collection \(\mathcal T\) of nonempty subsets of \(T\), containing \(T\) itself, such that any two members are either disjoint or nested. Each member \(A\) has a depth \(k(A)\), the length of the chain \(T=A_0\supsetneq A_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq A_{k(A)}=A\) of members above it, and a set of children, the members of depth \(k(A)+1\) contained in \(A\).

Definition 1 (Packing tree) A tree \(\mathcal T\) on \((T,d)\) is an \(\alpha\)-packing tree if for every member \(A\), \[
\operatorname{diam}(A)\leq c\,\alpha^{k(A)}\operatorname{diam}(T),
\] and any two children \(B,B'\) of \(A\) satisfy \(d(B,B')\geq\alpha^{k(A)+1}\operatorname{diam}(T)\), with \(c\) the constant of Lemma 1. For such a tree define \[
\gamma_2'(\mathcal T):=\inf_{T=A_0\supsetneq A_1\supsetneq\cdots}\ \sum_{k\geq0}\alpha^k\operatorname{diam}(T)\sqrt{\log\big(\#\text{children of }A_k\big)},
\] the infimum over all maximal chains in the tree, and \(\gamma_2'(T,d):=\sup_{\mathcal T}\gamma_2'(\mathcal T)\) over all \(\alpha\)-packing trees.

The functional \(\gamma_2'\) is dual to \(\gamma_2\) in shape. In \(\gamma_2\) one chooses nets and takes the worst point; in \(\gamma_2'\) one chooses a tree and takes the cheapest branch. A good tree branches heavily at every depth along every path, so that no path is cheap.

Theorem 1 (Trees bound the supremum from below) For every centered Gaussian process with separable canonical metric, \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}X_t\geq c''\,\gamma_2'(T,d).
\]







NoteProof





Let \(\mathcal T\) be a finite \(\alpha\)-packing tree; the general case follows by taking suprema over finite subtrees. We prove by downward induction on the depth that for every member \(A\), \[
\mathbb E\sup_{t\in A}X_t\geq c''\inf_{\text{chains from }A}\sum_{k\geq k(A)}\alpha^k\operatorname{diam}(T)\sqrt{\log(\#\text{children of }A_k)},
\] where the chains run \(A=A_{k(A)}\supsetneq A_{k(A)+1}\supsetneq\cdots\) to a leaf. For a leaf the right side is \(0\) and the left side is nonnegative, since \(X\) is centered. For a member \(A\) with children \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\), \(N\geq2\), the children have diameters at most \(c\alpha^{k(A)+1}\operatorname{diam}(T)\) and are pairwise at distance at least \(\varepsilon:=\alpha^{k(A)+1}\operatorname{diam}(T)\), so Lemma 1 applies with this \(\varepsilon\): \[
\mathbb E\sup_AX\geq c'\alpha^{k(A)+1}\operatorname{diam}(T)\sqrt{\log N}+\min_j\mathbb E\sup_{B_j}X .
\] By induction each \(\mathbb E\sup_{B_j}X\) dominates \(c''\) times the cheapest chain from \(B_j\), and the minimum over \(j\) of the cheapest chain from \(B_j\), plus the first term, is \(c''\) times the cheapest chain from \(A\) once \(c''\leq c'\alpha\). For a member with a single child the lemma is not needed, as \(\log1=0\) and the supremum over \(A\) dominates that over the child. Taking \(A=T\) finishes the proof.



The proof is Sudakov’s minoration applied once at every branching, with the remainders passed down the tree. In the language of the handwritten notes, the Gaussian process is being compared with a branching process: the comparison process \(Y\) of Lemma 1, iterated along the tree, is a Gaussian random walk on the tree in which each edge at depth \(k\) carries an independent Gaussian of size \(\alpha^k\operatorname{diam}(T)\), and \(\mathbb E\sup X\) dominates the expected maximum of this branching random walk over the ends of the tree. Lecture 10 introduced exactly this process, the Gaussian branching random walk, as an example.
What remains for the majorizing measure theorem is the purely metric statement \[
\gamma_2(T,d)\leq C\gamma_2'(T,d),
\tag{1}\] that a space with no expensive packing tree admits a cheap admissible sequence. This is the genuinely hard step of Talagrand’s theorem and we do not prove it. The argument in van Handel’s notes (Handel 2016) proceeds by showing that the functional \(G(A):=\mathbb E\sup_AX\), or abstractly any functional satisfying the growth inequality of Lemma 1, can be used to build the admissible sequence greedily, choosing at each stage the points where \(G\) is largest. Granting Equation 1, the chain \[
c\gamma_2(T,d)\leq c\,C\gamma_2'(T,d)\leq C'\,\mathbb E\sup X\leq C''\gamma_2(T,d)
\] is the majorizing measure theorem.

Handel, Ramon van. 2016. “Probability in High Dimension.” https://web.math.princeton.edu/~rvan/APC550.pdf.






NoteGaussian width through convex hulls





A different reformulation, from the handwritten notes of 2023, makes the theorem concrete for subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\). Suppose \(T\subseteq\operatorname{conv}\{t_1,t_2,\ldots\}\) for a sequence of points \(t_j\), and fix any \(s\in\mathbb R^n\). Since width ignores convex hulls and translations (Lecture 3), and the union bound of Lecture 4 gives \(\mathbb E\sup_j\langle g,t_j-s\rangle\leq C\sup_j\|t_j-s\|_2\sqrt{\log(j+1)}\) by comparing each \(\langle g,t_j-s\rangle\) with a Gaussian of variance \(\|t_j-s\|_2^2\) against the threshold \(\|t_j-s\|_2\sqrt{2\log(j+1)}\), one finds \[
w(T)\leq C\inf_{(t_j)}\ \inf_s\ \sup_j\|t_j-s\|_2\sqrt{\log(j+1)} .
\] Talagrand’s theorem implies that this is sharp: the right side is at most \(C'w(T)\) for every bounded \(T\). The proof takes an admissible sequence realizing \(\gamma_2(T)\leq Cw(T)\), writes each \(t\in T\) as \(t=s+\sum_k(t_k-t_{k-1})\) along its chain, and rescales the increments \(t_k-t_{k-1}\) by \(2^{k/2}d(t_{k-1},t_k)/w(T)\) so that the rescaled increments have \(\ell^1\)-summable coefficients and \(t\) becomes a convex combination of them; the enumerated rescaled increments are the \(t_j\), and there are at most \(2^{2^{k+1}}\) of them at stage \(k\), which is what produces the \(\sqrt{\log j}\). So in \(\mathbb R^n\) the width of \(T\) is, up to constants, the smallest scale at which \(T\) fits in the convex hull of a sequence of points whose distances from a common center decay like \(1/\sqrt{\log j}\).
